items.album: zakè ~ Tide Requiem for the Low Sea

items.body: Summer is ending. We must not say this out loud; it is a hard pill to swallow. For many people, summer has already ended; vacations are over, classes have begun, the water has cooled. zakè‘s Tide Requiem for the Low Sea is a long, slow, poignant goodbye, holding on until the very last moment, like the last bit of a small island before it is submerged. The physical representation is gorgeous: a double-sided picture disc, suitable for framing, showcasing photography by Tom Meluch (Benoît Pioulard). The images inspired both the music and their titles. One can imagine clinging to one of these peaks, like Blake Lively in “The Shallows,” albeit with more sadness than drama. Each side contains a single track, logging in at 22:46. The title track occupies Side A, ebbing in and out like the tide. Precious piano notes float atop the layered, undulating drones. Time seems be in suspension, although this is an illusion; it is simply passing slowly and inexorably from summer to autumn. Larger chords pass like behemoths in the sea, never quite surfacing, as much a feeling as they are a presence. How long can one hold on before succumbing to the sea? The answer should be six hours, the distance between high and low tides, and while we are not requesting a six-hour recording, it would be interesting to experience. A quarter-day at the beach allows for nuance, for incremental change that eventually grows extreme. “Tide Requiem for the Low Sea” seems to reflect the ocean at its lowest, before the rising tide, when one is aware that time is limited. The complementary “Crimson Covenant” is like a different viewpoint of a similar scene or like two persons comparing notes. Is the tide advancing or receding, and is the glass half full or half empty? If there is value to be found in each, might it also be applied to the changing seasons? The chords are darker, as one might expect from the title, which (likely coincidentally) is shared with an RPG. They advance and recede more swiftly, like the reduced interval between waves. The organ-like tones contribute elegance and gravity. Funeral offers music as a bridge between worlds; this piece suggests a similar metaphor. One of the unique curiosities of the record (as opposed to the download) is that the needle grows ever closer to an island peak, beginning at the outskirts as it alternately treads water and rests on land. The implication is that even the needle is seeking safety from the tide, and eventually finds it. The same may be true for the listener, leaving the seas of summer and landing safely on the shores of fall. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Review by tszirmay — Milanese quintet releases their third album, following their 2017 debut "Alight" and "Nautilus" which came two years later, both well received. The band continues to feature vocalist Francesco Lovari (whose English is as great as his lung capacity) , Alessandro Palmisano handling all matters guitar, Niccol� Gallani shuffling his keyboard arsenal while the family tandem of Loris Bersan on bass duties and Eric Bersan doing the drums and percussion chores. Nine years and no line-up changes, lovely move! "Wasted Potential" is a clever opening title that has zero bearing on the music proposed here, introducing the blustering keys, the thrilling voice, the rhythmic duo in full force and a shrugging guitar shroud, with less than 5 minutes, preciously condensed and intense. This is moder RPI, firmly ensconced in the schizoid 21st century, freshly brash and slash. A tremendous sizzler. Following that slap in the face with a sense of humour-laden "Please Be Gentle" is a proof positive that no one does drama better than our Italian Fratelli! Once again, the savvy interplay shows a team spirit that can only be admired (since the 'squadra' sucks lately, this is all one can have!), Gallani's moaning mellotron forging massive choral swoops, the bass and guitar smashing harshly and the percussive thuds very remote from tender facility. 2 shots, 2 goals, time for an epic! The 11 and a half minute long "The Case of the Silent Queen" evokes pastoral emanations of acoustic splendour (early Genesis and Anthony Phillips), the delicate arrangement increasing in intensity at a 'gentle' pace, the exuberant piano and drum cooperation making this a most flavoursome affair, the symphonics kicking in with romantic glee, as the mellotron keeps on glowing. The transitional variations are subtle, keeping the emotional impact well entrenched between the ears, dabbling bits of choir and thrashing cymbals awakening the soul. Suddenly, the not-too silent explosion arrives, led by an obsessive synthesizer loop, hushed vocal effects, and occasional axe-driven slashes that thunder without remorse. With all cylinders revving mightily, the lister's pulse cannot help racing forward into another realm of consciousness, no hint of filler or dross, just straight on musical theater for the demanding prog fan. Absolute master class demonstration. A little well-deserved respite is called for, after such a harrowing experience. "We Need to Talk" is exactly that, an effortless human grievance, we all have endured too many times. Heartbreak, heartache, loss, separation, distance, fate, called it what you will. The lyrics take their warranted place , upfront and center, as if "it was meant to be". A stunning vocal chorale, Palmisano shining on acoustic, Gallani burning on his keys, the Bersans keeping it all tightly wrapped in bliss. "Caged" is the other longer track, and as the title suggests , it's a heavily claustrophobic musical enclosure, the hyper piano possessed throughout, Lovari singing like an incarcerated victim of circumstance, no access to a phone or a ticket to freedom. We are stuck in limbo, and all alone. The screeching guitar solo secretes the angst for the longing of escape, the bass desperately searching for a way to open the locks, leading to the outside. When those damned mellotrons blow the roof off the penitentiary , the raging guitars in full collusion, the deed is done. Free at last. Maintaining the focus on the human condition, "The Day We Never Met" offers a jazzier vibe, weighed down by brooding e-piano and synth evolutions, a lovely contrast between melody and dissonance, but within a completely different style compared to the rest of the album. You may have guessed by now, and yes, the sturdy mellotron once again blows into the midst with thunderous resilience. Extraordinarily seductive. The title track puts this exceptional album to rest, a well-deserved siesta after a completely entertaining performance. As a fitting finale, the piece sort of encompasses the underlying thrill of the entire album, strengthening the beliefs in the talent presented here. Its everything one may want from modern day progressive rock. Please continue, and never get out of you strident grotto. 4.5 Anxious fibs

items.body: Review by alainPP — 1. "The Storm" captures a mood of melancholy?oozing guitar tones followed by percussive pounding and Riccardo's vintage keyboards launching the final solo. The lead guitar work is meltingly smooth and delicate?a real treat.2. "Sandsend" follows, with guitar supported by keyboards once again?Steve's guitar (the veteran member, if I'm not mistaken). It's a sweet, ambient, dreamy melody that casts a spell without overcomplicating things. Daniele's keyboard and percussion work is worth noting here.3. "Red Dragon" appeals immediately with its Celtic opening featuring bagpipes. I don't see a red dragon on the horizon, but rather a tune oscillating between Ireland, Scotland, and the Maghreb?a delicate blend of sounds that unite different worlds, which is what matters most. The guitars feel airy, plaintive, and hopeful, drifting into a dreamlike state. It features a radiant horn outro.4. "The Roaring Waves" arrives; if that isn't Steve playing, then it certainly sounds like him?delivering a magnificent, warm arpeggio over a chord progression reminiscent of classic Genesis (see if you can spot the influence). Those crystalline notes, plucked one by one, evoke an illustrious past. The track builds into a breathtaking solo?simple yet intense. The mood turns solemn, like a funeral march, with guitars?both acoustic and electric?softening before leading the listener into a neo-classical melodic passage; a gentle finale.5. "K-129" has a Gabriel-esque vibe?reminiscent of his world music work, specifically the *Birdy* soundtrack?creating an immersive, tribal atmosphere. There's a touch of 80s-era Genesis synth?or even Tangerine Dream?in that repetitive keyboard line. Daniele's dark percussion kicks off the guitar's wandering melody, building into a mantra-like crescendo. The track wouldn't be complete without that heart-wrenching solo?classic-era Marillion style: simple yet flawless.6. "The Black Sea" sees Leon on percussion?specifically a Hang drum with a touch of vintage vinyl crackle. The guitar tone is Floyd-esque and atmospheric, offering an enchanting, cinematic bluesy melody that feels like the perfect soundtrack for a TV series. Steve launches into a melancholic solo over a rising build-up?yet another one?that elevates the emotion to heavenly heights. It ends with a decrescendo accompanied by crackling sounds.7. "Pacific Coast Highway" marks a radical shift in sound; the American West comes alive with a festive, Western-rock vibe?think Chet Atkins?that makes you want to dance energetically and forget your age. Steve Hackett has a blast on the harmonica?at least you know it's him?while Riccardo treats us to an organ solo that harks back to the instrument's glory days. I detect a hint of Dire Straits in the fiery guitar work; my legs start moving and breaking into a dance. Halfway through, the acoustic guitar takes on a growly, Supertramp-esque edge before shifting into a linear guitar solo?not technical, just brimming with feeling and resonance. The finale is Oldfield-esque and pastoral, featuring a sensual, bucolic choir and a flute appearing out of nowhere to close the track.(3.5)

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — Marrow Deep by Mastodon is the band's strongest album in 12 years, with a new take on their sound with new members Nick Johnston & Jo�o Nogueira. The first album not to feature Brent Hinds after his departure then untimely death, lyrically the album deals with loss and the difficulties surrounding it. Overall lyrically it's some of their most poignant and creative. The added use of keyboards to their sound, while present before is now heightened with new member Jo�o Nogueira displaying some nice organ pedals and synth leads, while Nick Johnston has a similar style to the late Hinds, but has a uniqueness in his lead playing. While it's sad not to hear Hinds soulful vocals, Brann Dailor & Troy Sander's vocals are pretty impressive at times, but they do show weakness as well. Musically as always the band are impressive, with moments harkening back to their early Sludge years. While it's not perfect, it's a massive step forward for the band after a slight lull and obvious hardships. I'd give this a high 7 to low 8 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is Serpents For Dinner.

items.body: Review by Prog Dog — On my way over to finally dig into Neal Morse's album for my first review, I stumbled across an email I'd overlooked about his brother Alan's recent solo album. My curiosity got the better of me, and I was not disappointed. In fact, I feel like I've made a new guitar friend. Alan is a serious axe player and a very good songwriter to boot, and I've been quite taken by his soulful style and technique throughout this tastefully produced disc. This also proves the lyric from his title track, "Everyday Is Insane." Not really, but thank goodness for spontaneity.This is his second solo album (I haven't yet heard the first), and it's an impressive showcase of the man's very creative and understated solo work. There's very little repetitiveness or redundancy across this collection of eleven tunes, testifying to the abundance of raw source material he is drawing on here. If you're not fond of a song or a moment in a song, just wait a a minute and something completely fresh will come up next. After a few listens I find that I might not be in the mood for a track or two but I generally enjoy it all. He calls on a long list of friends and family to help out on various instruments and background vocals, and there's probably no shortage of familiar names here, least of all his brother Neal (by the way is Neal the big brother? or the little brother??). Tony Levin's presence caught my eye right away. And daughter Julia sings on "Making Up My Heart," which strikes me as a really sweet and personal touch, and a lovely reminder that the line of musical talent runs deep through the Morse family.This is essential listening for any serious Spock's Beard fan, of course, since that's Alan's main gig, and most of the band helps out.To me, though, this is a guitarist's album. Oh, wait, it's a real treat for drummers as well. The drum kits sound amazing and sit tight and loud in the mix throughout, and there's this ripper of a solo at the end of "Making Up My Heart". On the drum throne are some notable players: Simon Phillips, Jimmy Keegan, John Morse and, of course, Nick D'Virgilio.Alan isn't really lead-singer material in the sense of fronting a top-tier band on the world stage, but in a personable singer-songwriter setting, he's more than pleasant company for the ears.Since Alan is proficient in almost any stringed instrument, and he plays more than just guitar on the album. Not sure exactly how many but I heard bouzouki, cello, mandolin, and electric sitar. Not the most attractive album cover, but once you hear what's under the hood, you'll warm right up to it. There are almost party-rock vibes to some of the album, think Van Halen or that unmistakable '80s energy. I hear hints of classic Saga and perhaps '80s Rush as well. It's a thoroughly enjoyable listen for a guitarist and prog fan like me.Prog Dog score: 3.5 out of 5 &/or 3 out of 5 for the progarchives system.

items.excerpt: Review by Stefano61 — Genoa keeps its own kind of light, grey and pressed low over the water, the kind that makes a person feel the years passing even when nothing visible has moved. items.body: Review by Stefano61 — Genoa keeps its own kind of light, grey and pressed low over the water, the kind that makes a person feel the years passing even when nothing visible has moved. It was in this city, in 1896, that Eugenio Montale was born, long before he went looking elsewhere for words to describe what that light does to a life. He learned early that the sea does not console. It only continues.Something of that same continuing runs through the other Genoese story this record concerns.In 1970 a covers band called I Sagittari became something else when a young man not yet twenty, Ivano Fossati, joined on flute and voice. Delirium, they called themselves from then on, and within a year they had a hit single, Canto di Osanna, and a debut album, Dolce Acqua, poetic and strange enough that one of its songs lifted a dead man's monologue straight out of Spoon River.Then came Jesahel, sung at Sanremo in February of 1972, the five of them arriving, so the story goes, on a bus borrowed from Genoa's own football club. The song made them, for a season, the most hummed tune in the country.It also, by most honest accounts, did the band more harm than good. Barely a season later Fossati was called away to military service and never really came back, choosing instead a solo path that would make him one of the most respected songwriters Italy has produced, one who quietly left the stage in 2012 and has mostly been writing for others ever since.Even Jesahel would not lie still. Only a few years ago it found itself, entirely without anyone's asking, at the center of an international dispute over whether a much younger American voice had borrowed too freely from its melody, proof that these old Genoese tunes still travel further than 1972 could have guessed.An Englishman, Martin Grice, arrived on flute and saxophone to fill the silence Fossati left, and it was largely through him that the band found the sound of Delirium III, Viaggio negli Arcipelaghi del Tempo, a 1974 record already calling time itself an archipelago to be sailed through. Then, like most things Genoese, the band did not end so much as go quiet, and waited.It surfaces now as Delirium International Progressive Group, with Alessandro Corvaglia singing and adding guitar and keyboards, Michele Cusato on guitar, Fabio Chighini on bass, Enrico Tixi on drums.And there, still, are two threads running straight back to the beginning: Ettore Vigo, at the keyboards since that first 1970 lineup, and Martin Grice, on winds since he first stepped into Fossati's silence in 1972. Fifty four years is a long time to keep walking the same road.Sesta Strada Lungo il Tempo, released in May 2026, is in some sense a record about exactly that, about roads and the time that runs alongside them, about how a life, or a band, keeps its shape while everything around it changes.It does not chase anyone's attention. Winds and keyboards still carry most of the weight, as they always have, wrapped now around slower, more patient arrangements and character studies rather than manifestos. The people who populate it are not princes or supermen. They are drifters, the retired, the ones the road passes through rather than the ones who own it, watched with an affection that never curdles into pity.- Schiavo della Vilt�, slave to cowardice, twenty two minutes, nearly an entire vinyl side on its own, and the record's real argument. Cowardice here reads less like a single failing than a paralysis lived quietly for years, and the suite moves through it the way someone moves through an old house at night, recitation giving way without warning to symphonic light, a lyrical passage interrupted before it can settle, tension gathering, releasing, gathering again. It asks of the listener something like the patience Dolce Acqua once asked of a very different generation, back when sitting still with a record was still the ordinary way to spend an evening.- Io Clochard, I am a vagrant, the first human face the record offers once the suite's abstractions have passed, a song that studies a life lived entirely on the pavement with curiosity rather than judgment, the band's old melodic instinct returning gently instead of triumphantly.- Il Riposo del Pirata, the pirate's rest, an old adventurer finally still, the swagger gone out of him along with the urgency, the music settling exactly where its title promises, closer to elegy than to sea shanty.- Della Strada il Ritorno, the road's return, giving something back for once, a shorter piece answering the wandering of what came before with something like arrival, though never quite a homecoming.- Parole nel Vento, words in the wind, the close, scattering rather than gathering, the album ending not on a statement but on something nearer a shrug, which after everything before it feels like the most honest way to stop.Sesta Strada Lungo il Tempo does not try to be Dolce Acqua again, and it certainly does not try to repeat the accident of Jesahel. It knows, the way only musicians in their seventies can know, that the years do not grant a second youth, only a longer memory.What it offers instead is the sound of people who never really left the road, telling us, patiently, unhurriedly, what fifty five years of walking it has taught them. Anyone hoping for the old jolt of surprise will have to look elsewhere.Anyone willing to slow to the record's own pace will find a genuinely moving late chapter, faithful to everything the name Delirium has meant, from a bus borrowed for one unforgettable February evening to a Ligurian light that, exactly as Montale found, keeps its secrets simply by continuing. Highly recommended. My rating: 4,5/5

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — Singularity & Other Stories by Echoes & Signals is another great album from the Russian proggers that shows off great songwriting and technical ability, but it doesn't have the impact of the first album they released this year. While Solar saw the band put forward their strongest material to date, this album is similar in tone but I think it's the short length that brings it down. But having Leo Margarit provide drumming is a massive bonus, as his work with Pain Of Salvation is exceptional and it's just as impressive on this album. With creative use of synths and vocals, overall it still is a great presentation of the band's sound. I'd give this a mid 7 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is Singularity.

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — "Ys", named for the mythical and unfairly sunken Breton kingdom, isn't JOANNA NEWSOM channeling early Breton harpist Alan Stivell (who, like all good Bretons, reveres Ys"), and it isn't reimagining "The Milk Eyed Mender" in broad and long strokes, though simplistically that isn't utterly false. Its 5 tracks are not just epic in their length but in their subject matter and classically oriented arrangements deliberately drumkit deprived, the themes of family ties, co-dependency, love, aging and loss permeate the lyrics far better than the lyrics themselves permeate the consciousness. given her impossibly odd and arguably miraculous accent and phrasings. The subconscious, well that's another matter. I'm still processing, I think.Most of these works are afforded space in the early going, eventually accelerating into a breathless stream of consciousness, as impossible as this sounds. She is too unpolished to be rehearsed, and too polished to be unrehearsed, while similar could be said of the orchestral flourishes throughout, which seem to interject themselves desperately during the few 10-20 seconds interludes where she is presumably recouping respiratory capacity. Nothing here is weak but I especially the first for its lucid melody and the last for its approximation of a Baptist cum shaker hymn ("How can I keep from singing") through the lens of the American southeast. Don't expect to be grabbed and held from the outset. "Ys" requires a shedding of all your musical instincts to prejudge, judge, and judge some more after what should be enough devoted time, but its lyrical and musical messages preach patience and ruminations on aspects of life and lore over which sensitive folk have pored since music preceded language. It's not going to help our neuroses but it does, in a most whimsically idiosyncratic way, assure us we are not the only ones trying to make sense of it all.

items.body: (Colin Currie Group perform Steve Reich’s Quartet) Steve Reich’s ninetieth anniversary year would not be complete without a world premiere. Or two, as was the case in this evening’s all-Reich concert at Usher Hall, Edinburgh. There again, a Reich premiere would not be complete without the Colin Curry Group either, with Quartet (also on the programme) and Traveler’s Prayer previous co-commissions for Currie’s group. Forming part of this year’s Edinburgh International Festival, these two new compositions – Two Pianos and the stirring, spectacular In All Your Ways – appeared in either half of the program. More on that later. The evening began with Clapping Music, probably Reich’s most performed piece. Currie performed the piece on several occasions with Reich himself and recently told me that the experience was, in his words: ‘Completely surreal, yet not at all nerve-wrecking. Reich was a great person to take to the stage with, and I miss that interaction. I’m so glad I had that opportunity to perform with him.’ Certainly, fellow percussionist Owen Gunnell acquitted himself to the task at the Usher Hall’s reverberant acoustics, the duet executing the piece’s gradually shifting patterns with relaxed and consummate ease. This was followed by the first of two premieres. Two Pianos was originally composed by Reich in 2020, but for various reasons (the Pandemic amongst them) was held back until this year. Chorale-like in scope, the stately, slow-moving four-minute work revolved around a series of imposing harmonic pillars whose true significance was only completely revealed during a full and final statement at the end. Thereafter, the program took an upturn in energy and pace. The opening movement of the Radiohead-inspired Radio Rewrite for ensemble gained much from the way in which Curry – now conducting – managed to bind together its complex movable parts, his ensemble always alert to the music’s sudden shifts and tricky corners. The performance also managed to set the music’s propulsive qualities very effectively against more plangent moments heard during the second and fourth sections, while the closing movement rocked and rolled with more swagger and conviction than the Bon Jovi concert taking place down the road at the Murrayfield Stadium the same evening. Double Sextet provided a virtuosic end to the first half, with the first movement surging out of the blocks like a tearaway train and the third movement forever straining at the leash. The second half began much as the first had ended, this time with Quartet, pianists Philip Moore and Siwan Rhys and percussionists Currie and Gunnell locked tightly together throughout, sculpting the music’s peaks and troughs with power, accuracy, and precision. And so, to the evening’s highlight: Reich’s new work In All Your Ways. Scored for three sets of quartets (comprising woodwinds, percussion and strings), plus two pianos, the title is taken from Proverbs 3:6: ‘In all your ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct your paths.’ About as far removed from the composer’s recent Traveler’s Prayer as one could imagine, In All Your Ways was a revelation: Reich rethought and rewrought. Teeming with cascades of rising and falling lines that followed each other with almost breathless virtuosity and abandon, In All your Ways was far more linear in scope than what we have come to expect from this composer. Reich will often combine lines and layers vertically rather than horizontally. Once a rhythmic pattern and harmonic foundation is stated, he will then present and develop the material by gradually introducing interlocking lines and close canons above them. Reich’s musical conception is often therefore ‘simultaneous’ rather than ‘successive’, with patterns appearing as subdivisions of the beat. In All Your Ways appears to turn that idea on its head. These rhythmic subdivisions result in ever-shifting and ever-changing kaleidoscopic colours – a dizzying sequence of melodic spirals. Alongside these uplifting passages, a middle section provided a tender lyrical moment that seemed to draw on the melodic character of Reich’s opera The Cave. The work also ended with a beautiful moment where time appeared to stand still. Reich has noted that In All Your Ways is based on four rhythmic sections (sixteenths, eighths, quarters, triplets) alongside four harmonic areas, but the impression was of something more fluid, integrated, and organic. One cannot draw too many conclusions from one performance, of course, but In All Your Ways is a powerhouse of a piece that ranks alongside some of the composer’s other late masterpieces, such as Runner and Reich/Richter. If you missed the premiere, Colin Currie Group will also be performing In All Your Ways at the Concertgebouw, Amsterdam on September 19; Barbican, London on October 28; Philharmonie, Paris on November 22; and Großer Saal, Hamburg on December 4; with Canadian and US premieres featuring Soundstreams Canada and Ensemble Signal, Bang on a Can All-Stars and Brad Lubman, taking place on October 6 & 22 respectively. Not to be missed. The post Colin Currie Group Plays Steve Reich (Edinburgh International Festival, 28 August 2026) appeared first on Sequenza21.

items.album: Dark Electronic Duo The Axiom Divide Releases “The Halls Of Amenti : Remixes”
items.excerpt: The Axiom Divide begins with a grand premise: a doorway to hidden knowledge, an Egyptian afterlife reimagined as a psychological chamber where curiosity becomes a kind of initiation. On The Halls of Amenti: Remixes, that premise is handed to seven other producers and projects, each asked to rebuild the same architecture from a different angle. items.body: The Axiom Divide begins with a grand premise: a doorway to hidden knowledge, an Egyptian afterlife reimagined as a psychological chamber where curiosity becomes a kind of initiation. On The Halls of Amenti: Remixes, that premise is handed to seven other producers and projects, each asked to rebuild the same architecture from a different angle. The result is a remix collection with enough stylistic range to work in a club while preserving the philosophical charge at the center of the original. Jay Tye and Brent Heinze make an effective pairing because their histories already suggest two sides of the project. Tye, known for Soil & Eclipse, brings the gothic gravity and vocal drama; Heinze, whose work includes Probe 7 and the revived Darling Kandie with Franke “Groovie Mann” Nardiello, supplies a producer’s instinct for structure, movement, and electronic detail. Together, they push darkwave and futurepop toward something theatrical, with operatic and choral ideas hovering over machinery built for physical response. The remixers have plenty of material to dismantle. Razed in Black, Pygmy Children, Frontal Boundary, Fermion, I Am Consumer, and Dread Risks approach the source from separate corners of the dark electronic spectrum, turning the EP into a broad survey rather than a stack of minor variations. The sequencing helps: repeated encounters with The Halls of Amenti begin to resemble successive chambers, each version changing the perceived dimensions of the same symbolic room. Across the collection, solemnity and propulsion remain in productive tension, with melody acting as the connective thread. Repetition becomes conceptual, each mix opening another passage through a chamber the listener already recognizes and understands. The band explains the concept directly: “The symbolism behind…The Halls of Amenti references Egyptian lore to describe a metaphorical spiritual realm where a repository of forgotten knowledge welcomes an individual’s search for enlightenment,” says the band. “When the seeker of truth is deemed worthy, they are granted entry into this space to expand their mind and spirit. It speaks to our search for wisdom and personal discovery to enrich our lives.” That language could easily collapse under its own metaphysical density, yet the remix format keeps the record moving. Ideas of enlightenment, forgotten knowledge, and spiritual worthiness are translated into tempo, repetition, pressure, and release. Closing with Probe 7’s remix of Unrequited is a smart choice because it breaks the recursive spell of the title track and gives Heinze a final opportunity to refract The Axiom Divide through one of his own established identities. As an introduction to the project, The Halls of Amenti: Remixes presents Tye and Heinze as musicians interested in philosophy without sacrificing the body, treating the dance floor as another possible doorway into altered perception. Listen to The Halls Of Amenti: Remixes below and order the album here. items.body: Wrote my Senator, “Senator, what can you do?” But my dear Senator, you sold your soul to AIPAC too. There is something painfully American in the picture Stephen Bluhm draws in Emotional Plea: a man seated before a screen, writing senators, sending money, updating a résumé, scrolling through reports of strangers killed under another sky, while beneath these acts of conscience a disco beat keeps immaculate time. The first single from Work Crush, Bluhm’s quirky new project, takes political despair out of the arena of slogans and places it in the room where most people encounter it, alone with a telephone, a computer, a paycheck, and the knowledge that private life has become entangled with public cruelty. Bluhm, a longtime figure in New York’s Hudson Valley music community, gives that unease an unexpectedly elegant body. Recorded with Alex Wernquest at Basement Floods in Catskill, the song advances on a firm dance rhythm while synthesizers and clipped, Nile Rodgers-like guitar strokes gather around it. Mike Watt, the Minutemen co-founder whose bass playing carries muscle and wit, moves melodically through the track, making the low end feel conversational. Bluhm sings in a cultivated baritone whose theatrical clarity recalls The Magnetic Fields, The Divine Comedy, Joseph Keckler, and Paul Jabara. Aid disappears before reaching those who need it. A senator is accused of surrendering principle to political money. A technology worker recognizes that the product supporting his livelihood may also aid surveillance and imprisonment. Then the view widens toward civilians leaving for work or school beneath falling bombs, and the singer confronts the accident of birthplace separating his safety from their deaths. His question, “what is our dark destiny allowing this to be?” carries the exhausted bewilderment of someone discovering how citizenship, employment, consumption, and conscience can become knotted together. “With Emotional Plea, I’d never written an overtly political protest song, but I felt I couldn’t ignore in my writing what’s happening around us, with ICE, with Gaza, with the complacency and lack of compassion,” says Bluhm. “I usually write slowly, but this came together quickly because I felt it so urgently. Mike Watt is one of the funkiest bass players I know, and I knew he’d be perfect for the song. I’m grateful he agreed. He sent his bass track back within 24 hours. The man works furiously.” The final verse turns toward Christianity, reducing doctrine to an almost childlike attempt at moral imitation. There is humour in the image, though Bluhm sings without a wink; behind it stands an accusation that compassion has become easier to profess than practice. Listen to Emotional Plea below and order the single here. Emotional Plea by Work Crush Work Crush uses no generative AI, and musician-illustrator Steve Teare drew the cover image of a child playing with a toy military plane. It is a severe emblem for a song in which distant violence enters domestic life. After the orchestral intimacy of Bluhm’s Out of the Nowhere Into the Here, this new project finds him facing outward, fastening political dread to bass, beat, and melody, asking how comfortably anyone can dance while the world is simultaneously burning and flooding. What times we live in. items.excerpt: Chicago post-punk trio French Police released the double single “Super Over Drive” / “Silver” on 28 August 2026 through Interscope Records, with a video for each track. “Super Over Drive” and “Silver” are the band’s second release for the label, four weeks after the “Reptile” / “Japan” double single that opened the deal. items.body: Chicago post-punk trio French Police released the double single “Super Over Drive” / “Silver” on 28 August 2026 through Interscope Records, with a video for each track. “Super Over Drive” and “Silver” are the band’s second release for the label, four weeks after the “Reptile” / “Japan” double single that opened the deal. Chris Eichenseer directed both clips as a Someoddpilot Studios production and also shot the cover art. The “Super Over Drive” video puts the trio through a sepia-toned performance in which bodies blur into movement and faces appear and disappear. What French Police put on ‘Super Over Drive’ and ‘Silver’ “Super Over Drive” runs 3:22 and rides a driving bass line while Manny Herrera’s guitar cuts back into the arrangement from shifting angles. Brian Flores stretches his phrasing further than on earlier French Police tracks, holding notes past the point where the delivery stays composed. “Silver” runs 3:04, opens the arrangement out and leaves more space around the vocal, trading the first track’s defensiveness for a direct admission. Both tracks are on Spotify, Apple Music, Deezer and the other streaming services. No album has been announced around them, so they stand as the band’s second standalone Interscope single. The pairing follows “Reptile” / “Japan”, which arrived at the end of July 2026 and was the trio’s first release for a major label after seven years of self-released records and vinyl through independents. Side-Line reported that release in French Police signs to Interscope Records, releases ‘Reptile / Japan’ double single. French Police tour dates 2026 The trio play 26 North American dates between 11 September and 18 October 2026, closing at home in Chicago. 11 September 2026 – Detroit, MI, US – El Club 12 September 2026 – Toronto, ON, Canada – The Dance Cave 13 September 2026 – Montreal, QC, Canada – Les Foufounes Electriques 14 September 2026 – Boston, MA, US – Brighton Music Hall 17 September 2026 – Brooklyn, NY, US – 99 Scott Ave. 18 September 2026 – Philadelphia, PA, US – The Foundry at the Fillmore 19 September 2026 – Baltimore, MD, US – Baltimore Soundstage 21 September 2026 – Charlotte, NC, US – Neighborhood Theatre 22 September 2026 – Atlanta, GA, US – Terminal West 23 September 2026 – Tampa, FL, US – The Orpheum 25 September 2026 – Houston, TX, US – White Oak Music Hall 26 September 2026 – San Antonio, TX, US – Aztec Theatre 27 September 2026 – Dallas, TX, US – Trees 29 September 2026 – Albuquerque, NM, US – Sister 30 September 2026 – El Paso, TX, US – Lowbrow Palace 1 October 2026 – Phoenix, AZ, US – The Van Buren 2 October 2026 – Las Vegas, NV, US – The Portal at Area 15 3 October 2026 – Riverside, CA, US – Riverside Municipal Auditorium 4 October 2026 – Anaheim, CA, US – House of Blues 7 October 2026 – San Francisco, CA, US – August Hall 9 October 2026 – Seattle, WA, US – The Crocodile 10 October 2026 – Portland, OR, US – Wonder Ballroom 13 October 2026 – Salt Lake City, UT, US – Metro Music Hall 15 October 2026 – Denver, CO, US – The Oriental Theatre 17 October 2026 – Nashville, TN, US – The Pinnacle 18 October 2026 – Chicago, IL, US – Ramova Theatre About French Police Brian Flores founded French Police in Chicago in 2018. The Mexican-American singer, songwriter and guitarist writes in Spanish and English. Manny Herrera plays lead guitar and Rolando Donjuan plays bass. The trio bring a post-punk that mixes chorused guitar lines, driving bass and coldwave-leaning vocals, and they share a listener base with Lebanon Hanover, Molchat Doma and The Chameleons. The self-titled debut appeared in 2019, followed by the “Pedaleo Nocturno” EP the same year and the 15-track “Haunted Castle” in February 2020, which Icy Cold Records later pressed to CD. A dense run of self-released EPs and singles followed through 2021 and 2022, among them “Pensamiento Negro”, “Onyx” and “1995”, with “Club De Vampiros / Plant Based Girl” issued by Icy Cold Records in January 2022 and “Fumar / Hate Me” by Cruel Records that May. “Bleu” arrived in February 2023, and Audiotree released a live single and EP the following month. “Bully” came out on 26 January 2024, again self-released digitally with a vinyl edition through Icy Cold Records. Side-Line covered those European pressings in French Police launch limited European vinyl editions of ‘Bully’ and ‘Haunted Castle’, and Side-Line reviewed the album in French Police – Haunted Castle (Album – Icy Cold Records). The “Espera” EP followed in January 2025 with the singles “Sugar Killer” and “Libra” later that year, and Icy Cold Records collected earlier material on the “Essentials” CD in March 2026. The Interscope deal, announced at the end of July 2026, ends the self-released period; “Super Over Drive” and “Silver” are the first songs the band has put out since the tour was announced.

items.body: Neither of the two Andy Bell records due on 28 August 2026 came out. Extended Blue, the 21st-anniversary triple vinyl edition of his 2005 solo album “Electric Blue”, has been delayed because the original vinyl cut was not good enough and had to be re-cut. The double A-side 12-inch pairing new Manhattan Clique remixes of “Love Oneself” and “Delicious” was also held back for a second time. The Erasure Information Service, which announced the delay in its 28 August newsletter, has no new date for either. The album delay has an explanation. Writing in the newsletter, Richard of the Erasure Information Service stated that “the delay is down to the audio quality of the original vinyl cut not being quite up to scratch which meant the vinyl required a re-cut, which can take a bit of time”, and added that the new cut is believed to be finished and that he is waiting on the label for a date. The 12-inch has none. It was originally set for 14 August, then moved to 28 August, as Side-Line reported when the single was first put back. No reason has been given for either postponement. Both records remain on pre-order at Lexer Music and at UK vinyl retailers; the Lexer Music listings still carry the 28 August date. What is on ‘Extended Blue’ and the ‘Love Oneself’ 12-inch “Extended Blue” spreads eighteen tracks across three discs pressed in different shades of blue, adding four single b-sides to the original fourteen-track album, all of them on vinyl for the first time. Pre-orders include four art prints, and the first 500 also carry a bonus CD whose tracklist matches the vinyl. The double A-side 12-inch is pressed on pink vinyl and runs “Love Oneself (Manhattan Clique 2026 Extended New York Remix)”, “Love Oneself (Andy Bell Version)”, “Delicious (Manhattan Clique 2026 Extended London Remix)” and “Delicious (Andy Bell Version)”. Claudia Brücken of Propaganda sings on the album versions of both songs and co-wrote “Love Oneself”. Two “Electric Blue 21” t-shirts and a bundle of the 3LP, the 12-inch and a shirt are listed for the same date. Side-Line covered both records when they were announced on 15 July. The same newsletter carried one piece of forward news: the new Erasure album is finished. Richard wrote that “not only is the new Erasure album finished it also has a confirmed name, as do each of the tracks it contains”, and that the release timeline is still being worked out. No title, tracklist or date has been published. Erasure have no live dates scheduled. About Andy Bell Andy Bell has been the vocalist of Erasure since he answered Vince Clarke‘s advertisement and the pair formed the duo in 1985, after Clarke’s spells in Depeche Mode, Yazoo and The Assembly. Bell’s first solo album, “Electric Blue”, arrived on 3 October 2005 through Sanctuary Records and was made with Manhattan Clique, the remix and production duo of Philip Larsen and Chris Smith. The label collapsed around the release, and the record circulated thinly despite later CD and digital reissues. Bell has kept a parallel solo catalogue running since. Recent releases include the 2025 album “Ten Crowns”, trailed by the singles “Dance for Mercy” and “Heart’s A Liar” with Debbie Harry, and the “The Crown Jewels” 4-CD box set that expanded it, which was followed by “The Chance Won’t Come Again” with Tim Rice-Oxley. He discussed that record and his solo work in a 2025 Side-Line interview. “Extended Blue” was to be the first vinyl pressing “Electric Blue” has had since 2005; it now waits on a date from its label.

The duo mix gothic industrial rhythms
items.body: The Axiom Divide, the dark electronic project of Jay Tye and Brent Heinze, released the eight-track EP “The Halls of Amenti: Remixes” on 28 August 2026 through Re:Mission Entertainment. The EP reworks the project’s first single, taken from the forthcoming debut album “Halo Effect”, and carries remixes by Razed In Black, Frontal Boundary, Pygmy Children, Fermion, I Am Consumer and dread risks, plus a Probe 7 mix of a second song. The duo mix gothic industrial rhythms with operatic and choral parts. Tye handles vocals and synthesizers, Heinze plays synthesizers, and the pair produced, mixed and engineered the original versions themselves. Rodney Orpheus of The Cassandra Complex added production, and Rob Robinson mastered the record. The Halls of Amenti : Remixes by The Axiom Divide Tracklist and rollout of ‘The Halls of Amenti: Remixes’ Re:Mission staggered the release across August. The original mix went up on the label’s Bandcamp page first, the Razed In Black remix followed on 7 August, the Frontal Boundary remix on 14 August across digital platforms, and the full EP on 28 August. The label has not announced a release date for “Halo Effect”. The eight tracks run: “The Halls of Amenti” (Original Mix) “The Halls of Amenti” (Razed In Black Remix) “The Halls of Amenti” (Pygmy Children Remix) “The Halls of Amenti” (Frontal Boundary Remix) “The Halls of Amenti” (Fermion Remix) “The Halls of Amenti” (IAC Remix) “The Halls of Amenti” (dread risks Remix) “Unrequited” (Probe 7 Mix) Most of the remixers share the label. Razed In Black is the electronic project Romell Regulacion started in Hawaii in 1994 and later moved to Florida. Frontal Boundary is the Los Angeles industrial and EBM group founded by Brendin Ross, now on Alfa Matrix, whose “Burn” EP Side-Line covered in Frontal Boundary close ‘Failure’ cycle with ‘Burn’ EP. Pygmy Children is the Baltimore electro-industrial duo of brothers Pete and Brian Roper. Fermion is the New York pairing of Eric Shans and Augustine Backer, whose most recent Re:Mission release Side-Line reported in Fermion drops ‘Four Dimensions’ EP on Re:Mission Entertainment. dread risks is the Austin project covered in Austin duo dread risks return with ‘Where You Left’. Probe 7 is Heinze’s own long-running synth project, and it closes the EP with a mix of “Unrequited”. Tye explains the title through Egyptian lore rather than through the music. “The symbolism behind the single for ‘The Halls of Amenti’ references Egyptian lore to describe a metaphorical spiritual realm where a repository of forgotten knowledge welcomes an individual’s search for enlightenment,” the band stated. “When the seeker of truth is deemed worthy, they are granted entry into this space to expand their mind and spirit. It speaks to our search for wisdom and personal discovery to enrich our lives.” The EP is on Bandcamp and on the major streaming and download services. The original mix was a Bandcamp exclusive on its own and reaches the other platforms as the opening track here. About The Axiom Divide The Axiom Divide began as a solo project of Jay Tye, founder, lead vocalist and principal songwriter of the darkwave project Soil & Eclipse. Soil & Eclipse formed in Hawaii and released five albums through COP International: “Necromancy” in 1997, “Meridian” in 1999, “Archetype” in 2000, “Purity” in 2002 and “The Mirror” in 2008. Romell Regulacion of Razed In Black helped produce “Necromancy”, and Rodney Orpheus remixed on “Purity”, which makes both of this EP’s outside collaborators long-standing contacts rather than new ones. Tye invited synth producer Brent Heinze into the project. Heinze started Probe 7 in 1992 in Palm Springs, California, releasing albums including “Over & Out” in 2016, “Strange Angels” in 2019, “Parallel Universe 1” in 2021 and “Transference” in 2022. He has produced remixes for Information Society, The Cassandra Complex, Kirlian Camera, Gitane Demone and Dogtablet. He also revived Darling Kandie, the project first assembled in the late 1990s with William Tucker, alongside Franke “Groovie Mann” Nardiello of My Life With The Thrill Kill Kult, and the pair issued “NuAge Depression” in 2021 and “Tales From The Bone Phone” in 2022. Under the Axiom Divide name, Tye and Heinze first issued the self-released single “Generations” on 30 March 2022, which paired the single mix with remixes by Ashes Fallen, Probe 7 and Aggraux Kouture and a cover of Tones on Tail’s “Shakes”. “The Halls of Amenti” is their first release for Re:Mission Entertainment, the Oklahoma City label that has worked in industrial and dark electronic music since 2005. The remix EP is the last step before “Halo Effect”, the duo’s debut album.

items.body: Italian darkwave and post-punk trio Soft Scent release “No Flowers in June” on 21 September 2026, together with an official music video. It is the first single from “Mother’s Ruin”, the band’s second album and the follow-up to their 2024 debut “CHIMERA”. Pre-orders for a physical edition open on Bandcamp on 29 August 2026. That physical edition runs to fifty individually numbered CDs, self-released by the band. Each copy ships in a black envelope sealed with one of six flower wax seal designs, picked at random per copy, and comes with a printed art card carrying the artwork and credits. Who recorded ‘No Flowers in June’ Gianluca Lo Presti recorded the track at Loto Studio 2.0 in Filetto and at Logan Sound Space in Castelfidardo, Italy. Lo Presti also recorded Soft Scent’s debut album at the earlier Loto Studio. William Faith, a founding member of Faith and the Muse, mixed and mastered it at 13 Studio in Los Angeles. The song keeps the band’s darkwave and post-punk footing, with a restless bassline and insistent synthesizers. “Mother’s Ruin” is built as a concept album in the form of a travel book, moving between places, eras and stories. The title takes the Victorian nickname for gin, and the band set the record between comfort and destruction, escape and consequence. “No Flowers in June” deals with what is left once the escape is over. Soft Scent describe the song in one line: “Some endings don’t wait, they arrive before you do.” The artwork follows the album’s visual language, using dried and ceramic flowers marked with eyes modelled on Victorian Lover’s Eyes miniatures. No release date has been announced for “Mother’s Ruin”. About Soft Scent Soft Scent formed in Marche, Italy, in the summer of 2023, as a trio: Anna, who performs as MissLucifer, on vocals, keyboards and synthesizers; Enrico on drums and electronic drums; and Sara on bass and backing vocals. The band write and produce their own material. Their first single, “The Howl”, appeared in November 2023, followed by “No Wounds” in January 2024 and the title track “Chimera” that August. The debut album “CHIMERA” came out on 9 September 2024, running seven tracks: “Parasomnia”, “No Wounds (Album Mix)”, “Chimera”, “17:07”, a cover of Grauzone‘s “Wütendes Glas”, “The Howl (Album mix)” and “Susan and Sam”. Gianluca Lo Presti recorded it at Loto Studio in Filetto, and Maurizio “Icio” Baggio mixed and mastered it at La Distilleria Studios in Sarcedo. Tommaso Pompili added backing vocals and guitar to “The Howl”. The Polish label Bat-Cave Productions issued the CD in a six-panel digipack with a lyrics poster insert, and Manic Depression Records handled the vinyl. CHIMERA by Soft Scent Two remixes of the album tracks followed, by Ermete Lo Stige and Border. “No Flowers in June” is the band’s first new recording since, and the first material from the second album.

items.body: Toronto coldwave duo Traitrs released the official video for “I Was Ill, You Were Wrong” on 28 August 2026, a month before they open a ten-date US run in Dallas. The track first appeared as a standalone single on 28 November 2025 and became the second song on “POSSESSOR”, the fourth Traitrs album, issued through Furniture Records on 13 March 2026. Shawn Tucker directed the video and shot it in black and white on location in a studio warehouse in Hamilton, Ontario. Emmanuelle Vaughan plays the lead, Daniel Cherney worked as first assistant director, and Tucker and Cherney shared camera duties. What Shawn Tucker says about the ‘I Was Ill, You Were Wrong’ video Tucker connects the shoot to a death in his own life and to the way the album was written. “This album is incredibly personal for me because I’m still trying to make sense of a major loss in my own life,” he said. “When I directed this, the goal was to visualize death as this unstoppable force, almost like a terminal illness creeping through the body. It doesn’t care who you are; it just destroys. But I didn’t want the video to just be bleak. It’s about our internal fight.” The set is a black chamber with no walls, floor or horizon. Vaughan appears under a single overhead light, an oil-dark coating spreads across her hands, arms, back and throat, and she keeps moving until the frame empties. Tucker cast her after working with her on the earlier “Burn In Heaven” video and named Jonathan Glazer’s film “Under the Skin” as the reference for the space. “The void represented Ultimate Isolation perfectly and supports my visual theme of total isolation,” Tucker said. “There are no walls, no horizons, and no exit. The victims are entirely alone with their desires right before they are destroyed.” He described the shoot in plain terms: “It was all shot in one day on location in a small studio warehouse in Hamilton, Ontario, that took 7 hours.” When the song came out in November 2025, Tucker linked it to a shared recognition rather than a private one. “I felt that song connected me to everything and everyone, it is the one thing we all share and have in common,” he said. “It is also a wake up call to live the life you want to live. We only have one chance at this so go dance in the rain.” Traitrs ‘POSSESSOR’ formats and credits Traitrs recorded “POSSESSOR” at Wychwood in Toronto with long-time collaborator Josh Korody, who co-produced. Matt Colton mastered the album at Metropolis Mastering, and Tucker supplied the artwork. Furniture Records pressed the Canadian edition as a black LP limited to 400 copies, plus CD and a limited cassette. Icy Cold Records handled the first European edition on cream white vinyl with an insert, limited to 500 copies, and a CD digipak. Side-Line covered both announcements in Traitrs set March 13 release for fourth album ‘Possessor’ and confirm 2026 North American tour and Icy Cold to launch Traitrs ‘Possessor’ EU edition on cream white vinyl. The physical editions run ten tracks: “Burn In Heaven”, “I Was Ill, You Were Wrong”, “Seven Fictions”, “Cold Skin”, “Selfish Hunger”, “Prayertaker”, “Dream Drowning”, “Mourn”, “Japanese Picture Pony” and “Crawl”. “Burn In Heaven” got its own video on 12 March 2026, the day before the album arrived. Traitrs tour dates 2026 The US run opens on 29 September in Dallas and closes on 16 October in Washington, DC. 29 September 2026 – Dallas, TX, US – Club Dada 30 September 2026 – Austin, TX, US – Elysium 1 October 2026 – Pomona, CA, US – Flyway 6 October 2026 – Las Vegas, NV, US – The Dive Bar 8 October 2026 – Fresno, CA, US – Fulton 55 9 October 2026 – San José, CA, US – The Ritz 10 October 2026 – Sacramento, CA, US – The Starlet Room at Harlow’s 13 October 2026 – Raleigh, NC, US – The Pour House 14 October 2026 – Atlanta, GA, US – The Drunken Unicorn 16 October 2026 – Washington, DC, US – Pie Shop About Traitrs Traitrs formed in Toronto in late 2015 as a recording project built around Shawn Tucker on vocals and guitar and Sean-Patrick Nolan on keyboards and writing. Sessions with producer Josh Korody produced the debut “Rites and Ritual” in 2016, released on the Toronto label Pleasence Records as a cassette and reissued on CD and vinyl over the following years by Alchera Visions, Furniture Records and Icy Cold Records. “Butcher’s Coin” followed on 18 May 2018, issued jointly by Manic Depression, Alchera Visions and Pleasence Records. Its track “Thin Flesh” was used in Lionsgate’s 2024 remake of “The Crow”. The third album, “Horses in the Abattoir”, arrived on 19 November 2021 through Freakwave, with CD, cassette and coloured vinyl variants in 2021 and 2022 and a US reissue on Metropolis Records on opaque tangerine vinyl in October 2025. Touring has taken the duo through more than a dozen countries, including Wave-Gotik-Treffen, Castle Party and Canadian Music Week, plus dates with VNV Nation, Lebanon Hanover, She Past Away, Twin Tribes and Ultra Sunn. Side-Line reported on the 2024 North American shows in VNV Nation launches extra North American tour dates with Traitrs. After a four-year gap, the band returned in September 2025 with the “Burn In Heaven” single, followed by “I Was Ill, You Were Wrong” that November and “POSSESSOR” in March 2026. The new video is the second clip pulled from that album and lands as the autumn US dates approach.

items.body: The bassline on the new Death By Love track was recorded in a hotel room on a North American tour. Królowa Świata, out digitally on 28 August 2026, is the first original song the Polish-American duo have written in Polish, and it carries a guest bass part from Mario Usai of Clan Of Xymox. The gothic, industrial and trip-hop mix Death By Love brought to their debut album “444” is here pushed towards trance-styled synth sequencing. Królowa Świata by Death by Love The release runs four tracks: “Królowa Świata” (3:44), a “Psychotribe Psychoqueen Remix” of it (3:45), “Forest” (3:53) and a “Psychorchestra Remix” of “Forest” (4:02). Inga Habiba wrote the lyrics and sings; Peter Guellard handled synths and electric guitar; Usai played bass. Guellard produced and mastered the track at his Psychotribe Studio in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. The cover picture is by Robert Laska. How Death By Love built ‘Królowa Świata’ on the road The title translates as “Queen of the World”. Habiba addresses the song’s second person to herself rather than to a listener, and describes the writing that way: “these words are the whispers of my own subconscious, trying to break through the defensive armor I had built around myself.” Guellard began work on the track while touring the North American East Coast as a tech for Clan Of Xymox, carrying a portable rig and building around vocal takes Habiba had sent him. He cut the first guitar pass on Ronny Moorings‘ Rickenbacker. Usai then came into his hotel room, listened, and recorded the bass for the whole song. Guellard finished the arrangement at home, pairing fresh vocals from Habiba with the synth sequences. On writing in Polish, he commented: “Poland is our homeland, after all, even though at this point I’ve lived in the US longer than I ever lived there.” The video sets a vampire story in a mansion and a ballroom. Guellard built it from AI-generated imagery that he then edited and reworked with additional visual effects, the same method the duo used on their 2025 video for “Krakowski Spleen”. The track is on Bandcamp, Spotify and YouTube. About Death By Love Death By Love is a Polish-American project built around Polish singer-songwriter Inga Habiba and Polish-born, US-based producer, multi-instrumentalist and remix artist Peter Guellard. Habiba began performing in her teens with the new wave band Nizam, then fronted Monev, Ahimsa and the Warsaw gothic rock group Lorien, and worked with the folk-ethnic ensemble Habiarjan and the electronic act NUN Electro alongside her solo project CallMe. Guellard came up through the Polish goth band Blitzkrieg and later worked in the US dark-electronic underground with MACE, The Electric Hellfire Club, Venus in Furs and Dichro. A remix commission for NUN Electro’s “Hide” led to the pair working together on Habiba’s CallMe material, which became Death By Love. The duo signed to Distortion Productions and opened their catalogue with the three-track single “Strong Inside” at the end of January 2025. A Polish-language cover of Maanam’s “Krakowski Spleen”, with a video assembled from AI-generated visuals, followed in March 2025. They also appeared on COP International’s 75-track wildfire relief compilation “Los Angeles – From The Ashes”. Habiba and Guellard met in Warsaw in October 2024 to record “Strong Inside” and “Temros”, and completed the rest of the album across a year of file exchange between Europe and the United States. The single “Sellenno”, whose video was shot inside the disused Heinz ketchup factory in Pittsburgh, preceded the eleven-track concept album “444”, issued on Distortion Productions on CD and digital in February 2026 with a video for “Cosmic Power”. In July 2026 the duo put out “In Unity” as a set of remixes in tribute to the Polish act Wieloryb. “Królowa Świata” is their first release since.

items.body: It took no less than nine years for the new opus from Swiss band Sleepwalk to arrive. Founder Bruno Rush, assisted by Andreas Lehmann, has prepared 15 new tracks for “Dystopia”. An additional disc featuring no fewer than 17 is also available. To say the wait was long is an understatement, but it was certainly worth it. The result, “Dystopia”, is truly impressive. Sleepwalk’s compositions straddle the line between EBM and Dark-Electro. The songwriting is highly sophisticated, backed by an impressive sonic arsenal. The atmosphere is dark and the rhythms are danceable, while the tracks manage to be complex yet accessible. On the standout tracks—and there are quite a few—you can hear influences from the early Canadian EBM school; I am thinking specifically of the genius of Skinny Puppy. The opening tracks, in particular, absolutely blew me away and, in my opinion, rank among the best material Sleepwalk has ever produced. Given that the band has been active since 1992 and has a substantial back catalogue, the long wait has truly paid off. Sleepwalk hasn’t reinvented itself; rather, they seem to have taken a step back to reflect on their future direction. Lehmann’s haunting vocals fit the album’s atmosphere and genre perfectly. Towards the end, a few more magnificent tracks emerge, evoking the sound of Front Line Assembly. And then, of course, there’s the bonus disc, featuring 14 bands, each contributing a cover of a Sleepwalk song, plus three remixes by three different bands. It’s quite unusual to see so many bands featured with covers rather than remixes, and the least I can say is that it’s a very original idea—and it works. There’s also a fine lineup of artists assembled here, including labelmates such as Pyroline, Trilogy, T.A.N.K., Serpents, and Synaptic Defect, as well as EBM scene veterans such as Plastic Noise Experience, Brain Leisure, Individual Totem, R010R, Pantser Fabriek, To Avoid, and others. I have to say, there are some brilliant songs to be heard. Plastic Noise Experience does a fantastic job on “Afterlife,” and I should also mention Individual Totem, Synaptic Defect, and Nine Seconds. “Dystopia” is an album with a strong nostalgic streak, yet one that has been successfully translated into a powerful, contemporary sound: tormented EBM featuring some highly danceable tracks. Sleepwalk is back, and the world is going to know it. Side-Line announced the release in April 2026 in Sleepwalk return with ‘Dystopia’ 2CD on Electro Aggression Records, which listed the 2CD and digital editions and the full remix roster of the bonus disc “Interpretations”. (Rating:8½). Listen to “Devil In Disguise”: Devil in Disguise by Sleepwalk About Sleepwalk Sleepwalk are a dark electro and EBM act from Bern, Switzerland. The project was founded in 1992 by Oliver Spring and Bruno Ruch, Andreas Lehmann, and Charly of tEaR!doWn. The group started releasing material in the early 1990s, including “Immortal Disease” from 1994, the first album “Door To Insomnia…” in 1995 on Khazad-Dûm, “Black Diagnose” in 1999, “Torture Chamber” in 2002, “Retrospect 94-96 (The Early Years)” in 2003, and “Rapid Eye Movement” on Scanner in March 2004. By the mid-2000s the lineup had shifted. Oliver Spring left the band in 2005. The band later released the EP “Revenge Of The Lost” in 2011 and the concept album “Nibiru” in 2012, both on Scanner. Sleepwalk joined Electro Aggression Records to release “Tempus Vincit Omnia” on January 3, 2018. The band said they wanted to move back toward more classic dark electro with EBM influence after “Nibiru”. The Bandcamp-only digital set “Remakes”, issued on April 11, 2026, revisited older Sleepwalk tracks ahead of “Dystopia”, the 2CD set reviewed here.

items.body: Elizabeth Cotten wrote “Freight Train” as a child, around eleven or twelve, growing up near Chapel Hill, North Carolina. Left-handed, with no one around to tell her otherwise, she strung a guitar for a right-handed player and simply flipped it upside down, picking the bass lines with her fingers and the melody with her thumb: a reversed technique that later got its own name, Cotten picking. Rhiannon Giddens, who grew up in Greensboro, a few hours from where Cotten did, has recorded her own version of the song for Hope Is the Thing with Feathers, her upcoming album out September 18 on Nonesuch Records. The take strips down to just her voice and Dirk Powell‘s acoustic guitar, matching the bareness of Cotten’s own 1958 recording. Cotten grew up next to freight trains and said she used to watch them go by; the lyrics ask, plainly, to keep hearing that same sound after she’s dead, calling out to be buried close enough to hear “old Number Nine” roll past. The album itself was recorded live at The Cypress House in Breaux Bridge, Louisiana, with few overdubs. Giddens kept the sound of the room in the mix: talk between takes, feet on the floor. items.body: After the brutal heatwaves of August, the chilly depths of winter feel like a distant threat. But signs of the creeping cold are slowly emerging; cooling nights, the return of pumpkin spice, a dwindling tomato season. For those ready for the crisp return of colder weather, there’s Convulsif’s latest album, which is slowly unfolding like the change of seasons. Today, a new glimpse is unveiled. Fittingly, “A Torch Then Blaze” is something of a transitional track on Anatomy of Rage. A quick, bass-heavy interlude that emerges with sinister intent and lurching grooves spliced with grinding noise that connects the blistering first chapter with the funeral pyres of the middle tracks.While short, “A Torch Then Blaze” illustrates the fascinating juxtapositions created by Convulsif: maximalist experiments constrained within minimalist production, chaotic noise rock sharpened to a razor’s edge. Rather than embrace the massive production often found in experimental rock, Convulsif keeps their sound centered and brutally direct. Structure loses all meaning - songs range from 76 seconds to nearly 20 minutes - allowing tightly coiled grooves and jagged, jazzy rhythms to take control. The clarity creates a menacing beast of noise and abrasion, one that’s encapsulated by the brief warning siren of “A Torch Then Blaze” as it groans and explodes into noisy flames. Anatomy of Rage will be released on October 1, 2026. Pre-order on Bandcamp and follow the band via their website.

items.body: There are places that become so closely associated with geopolitics that it is easy to forget they are still inhabited landscapes, with their own geology, ecosystems and daily rhythms. Qeshm Island, in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran, is one such place. On Aerial Roots, Mo Farzaneh turns his attention to the island itself, drawing on field recordings made across its coastlines, villages, mountains and Hara mangrove forests. Wind, birds, water and traces of human activity are woven into electronics that grow directly from the environments he encountered. As Farzaneh explains in our interview, repeated visits taught him to recognise structures already present in the soundscape: changes in density across day and night, shifting winds and, above all, the tides, whose cycles repeat without ever producing exactly the same configuration. “Tabl” opens with wind carrying faint evidence of human presence through crackling environmental noise and birdsong, while sweeping shifts in pitch from a rising and falling wail give the piece a ghostly atmosphere. “Doulab” becomes more languid, bringing water and birds into sharper focus as an incantatory, revolving figure recalls the doulab, the traditional water wheel from which the piece takes its name. Circularity becomes still more pronounced on “Distant Memories”, where the movement of waves is translated into electronic material. Farzaneh describes the sea as an image of memory: each wave replaces the previous one while the underlying rhythm persists. The thirteen-minute “Aerial Roots” pushes this exchange further, playing with resonance until the natural ecosystem begins to resemble a negative imprint of its synthesised counterpart; towards the end, the environmental sounds gradually reclaim the foreground. “Sandstone Canyon”, meanwhile, introduces sharper sonic peaks and greater dynamic variation. The title catches something essential about Farzaneh’s method. Roots normally imply attachment to a particular ground; these roots have become airborne. His field recordings retain evidence of actual places and events, while percussive elements carry traces of particular practices, yet both can be detached, transformed and recomposed. Farzaneh noticed how Qeshm’s acoustic environment changes near piers and other centres of human activity, where species audible in quieter areas disappear beneath the noise of boats, while human sounds themselves can become strangely disembodied. Having moved to Qeshm after years in Tehran, he approaches the island as a stranger learning how to listen, deliberately resisting the temptation to interpret the lives he encounters. The album never turns these concerns into an environmental manifesto. Instead, vulnerability is embedded in its shifting cycles, where repetition always contains small changes and nothing remains sonically fixed. As Farzaneh writes of the Hara mangroves, this is “an ecosystem whose cycles have repeated here for thousands of years, now seeming more fragile than ever.” photo by Mo Farzaneh To find out more about the location and the recording process we asked Mo Farzaneh a few questions. Aerial Roots grew out of recordings made across Qeshm Island, from the Hara mangrove forests and coastline to mountains and villages, and you describe field recording less as collecting material than as a way of “spending time with a place”. Listening to the album, birds, water, wind and other environmental sounds often seem to determine the music’s rhythm and structure rather than simply provide atmosphere. How much did the environments themselves teach you how to compose? Were there moments when you found yourself following patterns already present in water, birdsong or wind rather than imposing a musical structure upon them? Yes, a lot. At the beginning of my field recording work, it was mostly the sound events themselves that caught my attention. But gradually I stopped thinking only about collecting raw material. I kept going back to the same places at different times, and I started noticing how the sound environment changed with the weather or with human activity. Those repeated visits made the place itself show me its rhythms and patterns. The way the density of sound shifted throughout the day and night was already a kind of musical structure. I just listened to it and tried to keep that structure in the composition. The electronic parts are basically my emotional and inner response to those patterns more like a conversation between the sounds of the place and my own reaction as someone who was there listening. I should also say that after years of living in Tehran, moving to Qeshm felt completely different. The unfamiliarity of that listening environment changed the way I hear things, and that shift still feels valuable to me. photo by Mo Farzaneh Your photographs repeatedly move between very large landscapes and extremely close observations of surfaces: eroded rock, cracked earth, tidal patterns in sand, mangrove roots, weathered walls. There is something similar in the music, where a recognisable environment can suddenly seem to dissolve into microscopic textures, drones and electronic detail. When you were photographing, recording and composing on Qeshm, did these different ways of looking and listening begin to influence one another? And do you see the photographs as documentation of the places behind Aerial Roots, or as another part of the same artistic work? Yes, I had already started photographing on the island before I began recording sound. Looking through the camera helped the direction of the project become clearer. Gradually I noticed that photography was affecting the sound sources I chose, and the other way around working on the sounds pushed me to take more photos, and more varied ones. Sometimes looking at a place through the camera while listening to it at the same time also changed how I structured the pieces or processed the sounds. Making this album and connecting with the place through these different ways made me want to share the other things I had collected too. That’s why I see the photographs as part of the work itself, not just documentation. They’re both telling the same experience, just from different angles. photo by Mo Farzaneh In your notes on the Hara mangroves, you describe an extraordinarily organised daily sound cycle: birds and other creatures gradually becoming more active, frogs joining the soundscape, crickets occupying the night, and the first bird at dawn effectively marking another transition. You also describe the ecosystem as having repeated these cycles for thousands of years while now appearing “more fragile than ever”. There is a comparable tension in Aerial Roots between repetition and constant small change. Did those ecological cycles provide a model for the album’s sense of musical time, and how consciously did the environmental vulnerability of Qeshm enter the work? Yes, but it was more a matter of gradually becoming aware of it. Because I was recording in the forest at different times of day and night, I started paying closer attention to how the environment was changing. I slowly noticed a recurring cycle things would repeat, but they were always slightly different. Even now, whenever I go back to those recordings, I hear something new. The changes weren’t just about day and night. The tides played a big role too. The activity of the creatures in the forest seemed to move with the tide, constantly shifting the sound. Places that at first seemed completely still were actually changing all the time. The wind direction could change several times in a day, the light would move across the water, and a bird I heard from one direction in the morning might come from somewhere else in the afternoon. Even something as repetitive as the daily cycle of the forest took on a slightly different shape each time. This gave me a strong sense of the tension between stability and constant small change a pattern that repeats without ever being exactly the same. That quality became something I paid attention to while working on the album. I tried to keep a similar feeling in the structure of the pieces. I was also constantly aware of how vulnerable Qeshm’s natural environment is in the face of human presence. The more I moved around the island, the clearer this became. Many of the quieter places, simply because they were further from busier areas, had a completely different sonic character. There were bird sounds you simply don’t hear near the piers, where the noise and activity of boats made the environment very different. That contrast stayed with me throughout the process. photo by Mo Farzaneh Memory seems to occupy an important place in Aerial Roots, most explicitly in the title “Distant Memories.” Field recording might initially appear to be an act of preservation — fixing a particular place and moment in time — yet your electronic processing allows those recordings to move away from their original form and acquire new associations. How do you understand the relationship between remembering and transforming in your work? Are you interested in preserving something of Qeshm as you experienced it, or in allowing those memories to change and acquire a new life through composition? Being part of this process made me think more about my relationship with places. No recording can fully represent a place. It can only capture one layer of the experience of being there tied to that specific day and time. What remains is a kind of sonic memory, and that memory keeps changing. When I enter an unfamiliar place, I usually slow down and listen before trying to understand what I’m hearing. Sound leaves more room for imagination than a fixed visual image. I start to experience the space less as something solid and more as something alive and constantly shifting. Listening to something unstable and fleeting feels closely connected to memory for me. A sound happens, disappears, and becomes part of what I remember. When I return to it later, I’m not necessarily hearing the same thing anymore. The recording is still there, but my relationship to it has changed. This became especially clear while working on “Distant Memories.” I took the continuous sound of the sea and worked with it in a way that keeps the underlying rhythm of the waves, but never lets any single wave stay for long. As one wave arrives, it gradually replaces the previous one, and then it too fades as the next one takes its place. In a way, the piece became an image of how memory works for me: something arrives, stays for a moment, and is slowly replaced. We don’t necessarily lose the memory completely, but its original form becomes more distant each time. The sea felt like a continuous memory the rhythm remains, but the individual waves are always temporary. That’s probably what interested me about it in the first place. photo by Mo Farzaneh Qeshm is not only an extraordinary natural environment but an island with a remarkably layered human history: inhabited since prehistoric times, shaped by successive empires and occupations, and for centuries positioned along maritime routes connecting Iran with India, China and East Africa. Your notes, however, approach the island at a much more intimate scale — people talking between houses, fishermen working on their nets, a goatherd calling in the morning, children cycling through a village, or someone inviting you into their home and offering you dates. What is your own personal relationship with Qeshm, and how much did you want Aerial Roots to engage not only with its landscapes and ecosystems but with the lives, histories and cultural memory of the people who inhabit them? My personal relationship with Qeshm is that of a stranger who’s gradually getting to know a place. Maybe that distance is why things that feel ordinary and everyday to the people who live there still feel fresh and worth noticing to me. That sense of newness is what made me want to listen to them and record them. As I spent time going around different villages and parts of the island, I started to sense something of the island’s history and collective memory in the rhythms of everyday life, rather than in its buildings or official stories. The way people adapt to the climate and their environment, and the kind of resilience in how they live, really stood out. The closer I listened, the harder it became to draw a clear line between the natural and human soundscapes of the island. For me, people’s lives were just as much a part of Qeshm’s soundscape as the mangroves or the sea. Since I was a stranger myself, still learning how to listen to this place and the people in it, I preferred not to explain or interpret their lives. I just let their presence stay part of my experience of the island. Maybe that’s why what I saw and heard found its way more into the sounds I chose and the overall atmosphere of the album than into talking about it directly. (Gianmarco Del Re)
