items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Horizons expand as if opening a door that leads neither to the past nor the future, though elements of both are present; this defines the character of Papangu, a Brazilian quintet that draws on numerous influences yet stands firmly on its own two feet. "Mau-Olhado" is an explosive opener with shades of Van der Graaf Generator, subverting time signatures and meters to make way for the vocal sections. "Colosso" brings us jazz-rock, but with vocals, lending it the feel of an auteur band; it is progressive, certainly fusion-oriented, and reminded me of the Argentine group Pez (in their prime). There are layered nuances and shifting moods that subtly overlap within the same track, featuring arrangements that are expertly crafted and perfectly placed. The parade of echoes continues, Gentle Giant makes an appearance, and the quintet shifts from pure jazz to a fierce, aggressive jazz-fusion that catches both the album and the listener off guard, never letting go."Taxidermia" continues the sonic revolution with the Moog front and center, yet the vocal sections are guttural, raw, and fierce, as if a stuffed animal had come to life and started speaking... like a dark sequence from a Lars von Trier film. However, classical piano notes bring light to the darkness, and a guitar with real character tests out a solo before the organ and that otherworldly, sepulchral voice return, creating a striking final contrast. There is a wealth of textures and colors, much like the album cover, which resembles an oil painting just waiting to be touched and felt.The album carries the scent of perfume... yet also the taste of earth, heaven, and hell. "Bode Expiat�rio" blends indigenous Brazilian sounds into that progressive cocktail; there are synthesizers, but also flute and harm�nica, elements of fire and air, alongside the kind of academic exploration associated with Egberto Gismonti.Celeste represents the other side of Brazil, that subtle, often overlooked facet found in the collaborations of Hermeto Pascoal and Edu Lobo or the early work of Sergio Mendes. Papangu surrounds themselves with an array of percussion and a vast arsenal of keyboards to craft a rich, surprisingly varied sound, much like the country's flora and fauna, which inevitably find their way into the compositions. The interplay of percussion continues in "Fechamento de Corpo," accompanied by guitar and flute, yet tradition and homage are disrupted by the intrusion of raw, high-energy rock sections; it is as if wild animals have once again taken control. It is in this stark contrast, which ultimately comes together seamlessly, that the band's spirit and artistic vision truly reside, all while incorporating technology to add textural depth.Calado (de Olho) plays with distortion, genre-blending, high-pitched vocals, and a mix of jazz and psychedelia in a way that reminded me of Gal Costa's early work, truly daring and accomplished, where the only rule was breaking with preconceptions.At times, Iamanakaru hints at certain Zeuhl-like facets, then plays with tradition at the start of "Afirma��o" before brazenly shifting into a markedly atonal progressive rock, almost ritualistic in nature. That is precisely where the magnetism of both the album and the band lies: they do not wait for the listener to come to them; instead, they come to us, right up to the farewell, which features a playful nod and a sort of Bossa Nova, but crafted in a space-age, symphonic style, as it could not have been otherwise.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The trio dynamic is further developed in this new foray into the ambiguous territory between rock, electronica, and the smooth yet steady interplay of synthesizers, guitar, and bass.This is how "Before Dawn" unfolds; as "Reach For Tomorrow" begins, a touch of improvisation, at once symphonic and psychedelic, weaves through the programmed tracks (which simultaneously mimic a choir). It would not be a stretch to detect echoes of both the classic style of Klaus Schulze like the modern style of Annie Clark from the band St. Vincent."Clouds" seems to feature a Mellotron, yet when the vibraphone and glockenspiel chime alongside the unhurried guitar notes, they evoke the quiet interludes found between Robert Fripp's dark, aggressive solos of the past, as if King Crimson had been stripped of its outer shell to reveal a vulnerable core usually kept protected. Above all, the approach taken in "The Only Way To Find You" is consistently tranquil and reflective, though perhaps not deeply profound, seemingly waiting to be imbued with whatever the listener brings to it. Like the rest of the album, "How Long Have You Remembered" reflects the marshmallow hues of the cover art, creating a somewhat surreal atmosphere; at times, James's style suggests a blend of the playful Talking Heads and the contrapuntal guitar work of R.E.M., while "Olen Yksin" features guest vocalist Laura Naukkarinen, whose ethereal presence underscores the postmodern aura of both the album and the trio.There is also a touch of Air, the French duo that successfully married electronica with 70s symphonic sounds. "Turn Turn, Round Here" returns with a hint of distortion to reassert the indie character of their sound; drifting amidst various textures, the track finds its natural rhythm, almost like a metronome, while the drums quicken and a Moog-like sound zigzags through the remainder of the song, heightening the dreamlike atmosphere.You can hear echoes of Kraftwerk, amidst the Rhodes piano and drums, with notes reminiscent of early computer sounds slipping through the interstices of a slowly built wall of sound, as subtle as the passage of time itself. That same sense of time accelerates electronically on "Don't Be Shy," where, much like Brian Eno, they manage to blend electronics with a rock sensibility, creating a piece that feels warm and emotive at times, even within a minimalist setting.

items.body: Review by Squonk19 — The latest album from Martin Springett's musical project, The Gardening Club, is called The Insubstantial Pageant, takes you on a wonderful, cinematic journey through time and place. Once again, the Toronto-based, ex-pat, musician, illustrator and author has conjured up a conceptual, narrative-driven album full of musical diversity and range, alongside a roster of talented musicians, many of whom have collaborated with him on previous albums.Based on an idea from Martin, with lyrics developed by Steve Bennett, the story of The Insubstantial Pageant revolves around a young woman whose father left the family when she was young and disappeared (for years he was rumoured to have been a spy). She embarks on a world-wide journey of discovery, following various clues as she travels to many different countries and getting glimpses of this enigmatic, ghostly figure. The storyline allows the band to explore many different musical cultures as we follow her travels - creating a genre-spanning instrumental spread, along with an intriguing mystery plot, full of suspense. As Bennett perceptively states: "Imagine Grahame Greene, Eric Ambler and John Le Carre locked in a studio with Procol Harum and Steely Dan."Martin's vocals and guitar work has crafted the diverse musical landscape complementing Steve's evocative lyrics, along with producer, guitarist and keyboardist Kevin Laliberte and Norm Macpherson's expressive orchestrations. Supported by Drew Birston on bass, and Rosendo Leon Arocha (Chendy) on drums and percussion - the lovely soprano vocals of Danie Friesen take us through the emotional sweep of the storyline. The music is progressive in nature, but informed by a range of styles, including folk, jazz, classical and ethnic elements, together with the group's blend of instrumentation, poetic lyricism and the stunning visual artistry that Martin provides with the CD booklet artwork.Ariel's Song starts the album's narrative in dreamy and ethereal fashion with Danie's haunting operatic vocals, acoustic guitar lines and gentle percussion - very much the prologue to The Insubstantial Pageant, where the daughter's quest to find her long lost father begins. Martin's distinctive vocals, joined later by Danie, merge with the acoustic guitar-led, lush instrumentation and vocal harmonies, with the rhythmic tempo ebbing and flowing, creating a darkly magical atmosphere. The music continues in a similar vein with two ballads, The Grey Men and then Geneva '46, as our protagonist follows the trail through captivating Cold War imagery, as Martin and Kevin's guitar and keyboards intertwine over the undulating drums. The former has a languid, almost desolate feel, whilst the latter one gradually picks up the pace and musical depth, with nice atmospheric electric guitar lines, as we picture a mysterious scene that would not be out of place in the classic film like The Third Man.Diary of a Grey Man draws us deeper into the story as we look at the scraps of an old diary to decipher the path that the daughter's father took. Martin and Danie's vocals mingle dreamily, with avant-garde touches, over Drew's eloquent fretless bass and elegant orchestrated string effects. Valparaiso '52 continues our journey as the story switches to post-colonial Chile - full of shadowy intrigue. There is some beautiful Spanish guitar patterns and misty harmonies over a more urgent, danceable beat, and Martin's vocals seemingly enacting a police interrogation of a shady diplomat, out of step with the new world order. The chorus is one of the catchiest on the album and stays long in the memory: "Our city - our rules. Nobody takes us for fools." We continue on our travels with the late-night blues/jazz of Chicago (South Side Story) which develops into a more funky, Steely Dan-like slab of soft rock, which provides a refreshing contrast - especially with some well-judged guitar and brass-like soloing.After the engaging, mid-way interlude of The Insubstantial Pageant (Reprise), Looking For Lorca continues the travelogue as we reach Spain - with Kevin's providing some lyrical flamenco-like guitar over a swaying gypsy rhythm. The lyrics express a feeling that the long quest for answers is more hopeful. The Hispanic influence continues with the sprightly A Sea of Emptiness (Cuban Sunset) before we arrive in the hot, arid, timeless vistas of North Africa, with Marrakech '64, with the vibrant sounds of Moroccan souks joining the atmospheric soundscapes and images of cream linen suited strangers with a Panama hat trawling through the back streets of the ancient city. The closing dynamic guitar soloing, siren-like vocals and resonating bass, work particularly well. You can imagine how much enjoyment Martin and the band had in trying the different musical styles as the storyline moved around the globe.East Meets West (Berlin 1979) follows the trail to the shadowy world of people around the Berlin Wall, just like scenes from a classic John Le Carre novel - and the trail seems to be getting warmer. The music enhances the cinematic imagery yet again, complementing the lyrics rather than dominating them. Martin's vocals do remind me of Andy Tillison of The Tangent at times, as well. A Long Distance Call has melancholic strings as the journey approaches the end, with A Return to the Park having a wistful, lush, orchestrated ambience with Danie's soaring operatic voice, marking the end of the story on a quiet park bench. It's been a long and varied quest for the daughter, both geographically and internally, but there is a warming sense of closure as the last notes play out.Martin Springett has conjured up an introspective musical story as evocative as any of his famed illustrations with The Insubstantial Pageant, the latest album from his musical project, The Gardening Club. With a diverse, but suitably measured, musical palette of genres and styles complementing Steve Bennett's lyrics, we follow an engaging story of a daughter's quest for a long-lost father through the dark corners of the post-war world. Progressive in scope rather than prog rock in nature, there is much to savour in the layered synergy between the acoustic and electric guitars, keyboards, bass, drums and varied lead vocals and harmonies. It is a refreshingly singular album that would please any listeners who value lyrically driven albums with thoughtful, nuanced musical themes. An album whose overall theme would make a wonderful book or film ? but one that remains addictively captivating and cinematic in musical form. Dedicated to the late Canadian saxophonist Wayne Kozak, is this album Martin's most ambitious and successful work to date? Quite possibly?(From The Progressive Aspect)

items.body: Review by yarstruly — Clicked 5, but really 4.5Simultaneosly posted on my blog: Scott's Song by Song Spotlights, with links to buy and listen.Lonely Robot is a solo project of Irish prog guitarist extraordinaire John Mitchell. John's resume is amazing! John is or has been a member of It Bites, Arena, Frost*, Kino, A, The Urbane, and Asia. His list of guest appearances is far too long to list here, but I know he is on Karmakanic's latest album Transmutation. In addition to being an amazing, in demand guitarist, John is a wonderful singer as well. John has been releasing his solo material as "Lonely Robot" since 2015's "Please Come Home". "The Big Dream" (2017), "Under Stars" (2019), "Feelings are Good" (2020), "A Model Life" (2022) all followed, and I have enjoyed material from every one of them. Now, John is set to release "An Ending" on September 11, 2026. As the title implies, John intends this to be the final Lonely Robot album.Here are the credits:- John Mitchell / vocals, guitars, bass guitar, keyboards- Craig Blundell / drumsWith:- Jez Fielder / guitars (8,9) Craig Blundell is best known for his work with Frost* and Steven Wilson's solo material. Among other things, Jez Fielder is known for his band Indigo Down. Additionally, the album has fantastic artwork from Graeme Purdy Bell. The album comes courtesy of John's PR rep, Sarah Ewing. As always, I receive no further compensation, and I call it like I hear it. As per my usual method, this is a cold listen.Track 1 - This World Window (2:26) The track fades in with synth sounds playing a rhythmic pattern. John's vocals soon join in singing about being a Lonely Robot who's come to say goodbye. There are some wonderful harmonies along the way. It ends with some sound effects and spoken words I can't make out. A bittersweet opener.Track 2 - Show the Way (4:39)A keyboard pattern with a sustained flute-like sound starts us off, then a fast energetic beat kicks in. There are some odd-meters changing things up. I love the vocal melody in the pre-chorus. Nice harmonies in the chorus. The energy in this one is awesome. There is a part where most of the instruments drop out at 2:40 or so. The synth motif is very proggy! John's soaring guitar solo hits at 3:45 and it's wonderful! After another chorus, the song concludes with an a cappella stating of the title. Fantastic track.Track 3 - Back to the Middle (3:51)Keys and a marching snare drum are quickly joined by the full band and John's lead guitar for the intro. The rhythm is a strong mid-tempo groove. The sound is full and rich. I love his voice tone in the opening line "Well, I'm facing hollow promises"... This has a slightly 80s sound to it, lots of reverb and expansive tones. The chorus has a nice hook. His voice reminds me of John Wetton or Greg Lake. A beautiful guitar solo comes in during the middle of the song. The song fades out as it began with the keys and marching snare drum. Wonderful song. Dare I say it?radio friendly?Track 4 - In Ocean Light (5:59)A music box-type tone and sound effects initiate things here. Then it's like a piano ballad with orchestra and mellotron tones. This is a ballad. Subtle drums and bass enter on the second verse. I love the delays when he sings the title line. The intensity is slowly building throughout the song. The guitar solo begins at around 3:45; very melodic. The extended solo develops nicely and becomes more complex and assertive as it goes. There is certainly a David Gilmour influence, but with an occasional fast run. The solo runs all the way until the end of the song. Guitar lovers will really like this one! (And I am a guitar player.)Track 5 - Ad Astra (4:53)The title is Latin for "to the stars". An orchestrated synth part with a spoken-word voice, as if from an interstellar radio transmission, describing the vastness of space, and that some planets are in the "inhabitable zone". A mid-tempo 6-8 beat, driven by Blundell's rimshot drum beat keeps the song moving as Mitchell sings. The choruses build the tension. At around 2:40 there is a brief quiet part before John's guitar playing takes over. Following the solo, the accompaniment is minimal before everything returns soon after. Strong track.Track 6 - Where in the World (3:45)This one fades in with a faster tempo pattern. I like the guitar countermelody over the rhythmic soundscape. The vocals begin with minimal keyboard accompaniment; it reminds me of Asia's "Wildest Dreams". Of course, Mitchell is in the current version of Geoff Downes' Asia (not to be confused with John Payne's Asia), but not as lead vocalist but as the guitarist, but his vocal tone and style would fill that niche nicely. The chorus has a lot of forward momentum. The song cuts loose even more in the bridge at around 2:30. Another masterful guitar solo follows. Awesome track!Track 7 - Twin Suns (6:22)This is the longest track on the album. An ominous drone starts us off, soon joined by a cool rhythm pattern. The vocals come in at around 40 seconds. The verses are in 6-4 and I believe we are in 5-4 during the choruses, if I am counting correctly. A short guitar solo happens between the first chorus and second verse. A longer guitar solo follows after the second chorus. I love the refrain of "Twin suns in the distance" as the song fades out. Cool song!Track 8 - The River (5:55)A short, but strong intro quickly gives way to the first verse, which is accompanied by acoustic guitar strumming and electric piano. The rhythm section kicks in at around one minute in, following the first verse. I like Blundell's drum patterns on this song (and throughout the album, for that matter). The acoustic sections give me Pink Floyd vibes. The guitar solo comes in at around 4 minutes. A bridge follows. I like the overall arrangement of this song. The song closes with the line "on and on, the river's just begun". Good one.Track 9 - Rearview (4:39)This one starts directly after "The River". Some synth tones give way to a "tribal" type of drum beat, The band joins onto his foundation. Nice key change going into the chorus. I love the production on this album. The melodies here are complex and take some unexpected turns. Awesome drum fill from Blundell as the guitar solo concludes at around 3:55. An intriguing song that will probably require repeated listenings to fully digest. Track 10 - Bending Light (5:37)An unusual, distorted synth tone plays arpeggios and Mitchell enters on vocals with a drum machine rhythm. Blundell gives a real drum and cymbal accent a couple of times. Mitchell's voice sounds anguished. A spoken part is low in the mix, discussing relationships. This is another one that will take multiple listens to fully digest, lyrically, but I am drawn in. Blundell joins in fully at around 3 minutes. The guitar solo begins at around 3:45. His playing and his voice are very expressive. Sound effects and the drum machine pattern close it out. Haunting track. Track 11 - The Iron Sea (3:50)Ocean shore sounds fittingly start us off here. Sound effects give an uneasy effect. Michell's voice reminds me more of Peter Gabriel here. The music builds up and explodes at around 2 minutes with power chords. This one reminds me a little of "Space-Dye Vest" from Dream Theater, at least in its vibe. That is a favorite DT song of mine, so consider that a compliment.Track 12 - Oblique (3:23) A simple but slightly disturbing piano pattern in 6-8 stars off the final proper album song. Mitchell's vocals are bittersweet here, especially as he sings "Sorry, my heart breaks gently". I believe we are saying goodbye to the "Lonely Robot"...I'm not crying?you're crying"...Track 13 - Synthetic (Vinyl only Bonus Track) (3:22)A sustained synth chord starts us off then John joins in on vocals. There are subtle drums. This is another bittersweet song, with a haunting, yet hopeful vibe. Mostly keys and vocals.OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:A wonderful close to John Mitchell's Lonely Robot series of albums. There is a reason that John is so in demand as a guitarist as well as vocalist. While there are lots of synths and electronic sounds, his guitar and vocal parts bring a sense of warmth and humanity. Blundell's drumming adds a great sense of dimension to the sound as well. I really enjoyed that. There is a lot of depth in the lyrics that will take me some time to fully wrap my mind around, as I am a music first, lyrics later kind of guy. But it is a very strong album that fans of Pink Floyd/David Gilmour and prog/mainstream rock hybrids will truly enjoy. I give it 4.5 out of 5 stars (90%).

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 984Porcupine Tree is an English progressive rock band that was formed in 1987 in Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire. The fourth studio album of Porcupine Tree "Signify" that was released in 1996 is their first album with a fixed line up. Steven Wilson previously used various musicians to shape his compositions. "Signify" shows a clear transition phase from the band with the long instrumental tracks and lots of musical experiments to the more song orientated band. "Signify" presents a more mature approach than on "The Sky Moves Sideways", which doesn't mean better, having a stronger mix of styles. This is a relaxed work, generally slow and that doesn't have many hooks for the listener to grab on to. Its psychedelic sound is more ambient than ever, but I think isn't as deep as the wonderful "The Sky Moves Sideways".The line up on "Signify" is Steven Wilson (vocals, electric and acoustic guitars, samplers, tapes, organ, Mellotron, piano, drum programming, chimes and musical box), Richard Barbieri (piano, Hammond organ, tapes, sequencers and synthesizers Prophet-V and Roland System 700), Colin Edwin (bass and double bass guitars) and Chris Maitland (vocals, drums, cymbals, percussion, drum loops and keyboards. The work had the participation of Terumi (vocals) too.The original version of "Signify" has twelve tracks. "Signify" begins with "Bornlivedie" in which a narrator invites us to make ourselves comfortable to enjoy a soundscape that culminates with a female voice saying "Signify". "Signify" is the title track, where we actually can say that the album begins. It's an incredible paranoia inducing track, a hard riff, a pure electronic wonder and where a simple distorted solo from Wilson gives the atmosphere and rhythm. "The Sleep Of No Dreaming", as most of the songs of the album, has a very dark and brooding feel with lyrics chilling and sharp. It's a contrasting composition with the previous instrumental with quiet chords on the keyboards that set the dreamy mood for the track. "Pagan" is a quick transitory piece. It's a soundscape, an atmospheric piece, a guiding element between one theme and another. "Waiting Phase One" and "Waiting Phase Two" take up just over ten minutes. The first part starts with some acoustic chords and a few beats on the bass drum creating a peaceful moment, a kind of different peace. The second part is tribally enchanting due to the variety of sounds that emerge from it with a brief phrase on the piano and the tuneful touch on the guitar. The percussion and drums stand out within this psychedelic trance. "Sever" is where the harder progressive rock meets the electronic music. Maitland and Edwin are simply spectacular. It has a great chorus, with distorted voices crying out in despair, which makes this song another highlight on the album. "Idiot Prayer" has a pure electronic ambient. The band again approaches a different style and shows how eclectic they can be. Over a danceable rhythm, the guitar and keyboards move gracefully equally supported by an attractive percussion. "Every Home Is Wired" is a song that sounds more like a "Stupid Dream" or a "Lightbulb Sun" track. Here we have guitar and dreamlike keyboards under some echoing voices. Again the band is showing that this album can have it all. "Intermediate Jesus" is one of the biggest tracks on the album. It sounds like a kind of a jam that was included in the final material. This is an interesting instrumental, mostly improvisation, the only collective composition on the album. "Light Mass Prayers" is another ambient piece, but much longer than "Pagan". It has an atmospheric beginning, an ambient sound mainly through the keyboards. It's an exploration and experimentation by Wilson. "Dark Matter" is the lengthiest track on the album. It has some of the most brutal lyrics on the album, takes us out with an epic solo and some recollection and deep thought. This beautiful song, so dreamy and so awakening closes the album in a great way.The expanded remastered edition of "Signify" has 2 CD's. It comes with a bonus disc. The supplemental CD consists of demos recorded by the band between 1995-1996. This limited edition contains some extremely well developed, but still rough-on-the-edges demos and outtakes of "Signify". If you have any doubt about the quality of those tracks, rest assured. You don't get filler material here, but a fine complete album, which can hold a candle to the original release.Conclusion: Porcupine Tree occupies a very special place in the field of modern progressive rock and "Signify" is a great example of that. In reality, what we have here is a great addition to any progressive music collection. Basically all facets of the band on only one album are performed in high performance and with rich musicality. Overall, I loved the album and it's a great transition from their psychedelic space rock era, to a more modern progressive rock style which they later perfected. As I said before, "Signify" is the first Porcupine Tree's album where they sound like a band and not a Wilson's "vanity" project. It's a work where they forge their own unique sound and the foundation of their future albums "Stupid Dream" and "In Absentia". Nevertheless, regardless of it not being the best Porcupine Tree's album, this is a highly recommended work. Both challenging and accessible, this album surely has won over some new fans.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

items.body: Review by alainPP — Gandalf's Fist offers a genre-defying brand of conceptual progressive rock, characterized by a dreamlike atmosphere, operatic storytelling, and a distinctive rock sound."The Lamplighter Suite" revisits the opening of *The Clockwork Prologue*, delivering a solid fifteen minutes of eclectic prog rock. It encompasses neo-prog, heavy metal, and folk?the full spectrum of this unclassifiable band. This remastered piece features imposing transitions, a grandiloquent scope, and a majestic finale driven by pompous orchestration backing Keri's signature vocals.The subsequent sections are drawn from their benchmark album *The Clockwork Fable*; "Parts I-VIII" sees Melissa's vocals stepping into this hidden rock opera. The original album featured guests like Blaze Bayley and spanned over three hours, complete with heavy, crushing metal breaks?though here, we get a condensed fifteen-minute version.The "Parts IX-XIII" sequence features Arjen as a guest?acting more as narrator than singer, evoking the Ayreon sound?alongside Melissa's enchanting, sultry, angelic vocals. The mood shifts from medieval-folk gentleness to doom metal reminiscent of Black Sabbath. The finale is sweeter and remains wonderfully eclectic, continuing to transport the listener into a symphonic, Tolkien-esque world.The conclusion comes with the brief "Parts XIV-XV," featuring Luke on vocals and a solemn, excellent melody with Middle Eastern and Japanese influences.Gandalf's Fist celebrates its sprawling 2016 album by weaving together its sixteen musical chapters; it serves as a "fake" compilation that highlights this complete, uninterrupted, masterful, and admirable work. Excellent. (4.5)

items.body: The Prom on August 20 commemorated the centennial of Miles Davis’s birth. Davis was undoubtedly one of the greatest and most important musicians of the 20th century, but he was not a composer and not just a performer. He was a composing performer, who probably never played the same thing the same way twice. His playing is known to many people, just about everybody now, through his recordings, which were a single example of how he would have done something, and which are also very much a product of his work with arrangers, most especially Gil Evans. It is their collaboration which is known through recordings such as Miles Ahead, Sketches of Spain, and Porgy and Bess. But those recordings can’t just be recreated, nor would anybody want them to be. So the audience for this Prom heard Ambrose Akinmusire, trumpet, Sam Harris, piano, Harish Raghavan, bass, Kendrick Scott, drums, along with the BBC Concert Orchestra, conducted by Miho Hazama, all of them very very fine and wonderful musicians, evoking, through their own playing and different arrangements, which were nonetheless evocations of the famous arrangements, mostly by Gil Evans, the magical quality of Davis’s recordings, and for the most part it all succeeded wonderfully. (For this listener, for instance, the performance of My Ship came far short of the character and quality of Davis’s recording). The program for the concert had a very detailed and informative account of Davis’s life and the development of his career by Alyn Shipton. It also included a short interview with Ambrose Akinmusire about Davis’s influence on succeeding musicians and, in fact, on some of the issues discussed above. It was altogether a very enjoyable evening of music making, celebrating Davis’s creations and achievements.The bulk of the Prom two nights earlier, presented by the BBC Symphony Orchestra, conducted by Cristian Mãelaru, was occupied by the Symphony No. 10 by Shostakovich. That work was preceded, though, by Skyline, a concerto for three percussionists and timpani by Édith Canat de Chizy, which was a BBC co-commission and which was receiving its UK premiere. The soloists were Lucy Landymore, Emma Arden, Delia Stevens, and Richard Cartidge. Skyline over its twenty minute length traces five stages from the emerging of the universe from blackness, through the dawn of the cosmos, the birth of different kinds of starts, the explosion and rhythm of pulsars, to the death of the cosmos. The four soloists were positioned around the orchestra which in fact became a sort of amplifier of their sounds and, in fact, of the argument of the work. The work was continually compelling in its sounds and riveting in its progress. Canat de Chizy was a composers I knew nothing about before this encounter and one who I will look out for going forward. Probably due to the very oppressive cultural climate of the last years of Stalin’s rule in Russia, Shostakovich wrote, or at least, released very few major works during that time. The Tenth Symphony appeared a few months after Stalin’s death, and it was taken, and is probably still taken, as a commentary on that situation. The very abrasive scherzo, the second movement was apparently intended as a portrait of Stalin. This performance presented the work to its fullest advantage. The advertising and presentation of this concert, which mentioned the Shostakovich only and the Canat de Chizy not at all, is an example of how the BBC is currently presenting these concerts in general. In this case, one might have assumed that the Shostakovich was the only piece on the concert, and one would have had to dig deep, or at least deeper, to find that there was another piece on the concert, and that it was by a living composer and had been commissioned by the BBC. The inclusion of newer pieces used to be celebrated; now it’s more or less hidden. The tactic seems pretty clear. One wonders if this particular approach to things really produces a larger audience, which is presumably the goal. In a similar manner, the Prom of the 21st of August, presented by The BBC Philharmonic, conducted by Anja Bihlmaier, with soloists tenor Clay Hiley and mezzo soprano Jamie Barton, only promoted the final work on the concert, Das Lied von der Erde by Mahler, without mentioning the pieces on the first half of the concert, the Haydn Farewell Symphony (No. 45, in f sharp minor) and Mosaic by Bushra El-Turk. El-Turk is a British composer of Lebanese descent whose work has been very much involved with the integration of eastern and western musical elements. Mosaic, lasting 8 minutes, which was receiving its first performance at the Proms, was commissioned by the Manchester Camerata for a season which explored the question of cross-pollination of ideas between cultures. It’s compelling shape is one of increasing activity and intensity from the beginning to a climactic point where the bottom falls out of things and there is a very quiet music which evokes Byzantine chant which concludes the piece after a very brief reminiscence of the previous activity. It was a fine beginning to a concert of equally compelling pieces, all of them masterfully performed. The post BBC Proms Miles Davis, Canat de Chizy, El-Turk, Shostakovich appeared first on Sequenza21.

items.album: “Intimately rustic”: Motvind festival reviewed
items.excerpt: What began as an arts funding protest has grown into a constellation of site-specific performances at this rural Norwegian event, writes Peter Margasak in The Wire 511 Motvind Various venues, Rollag, Norway Thanks to limited resources and modest aims, small summer festivals all across Europe adapt a simple formula: programme a couple of touring acts and round things out with local musicians. items.body: What began as an arts funding protest has grown into a constellation of site-specific performances at this rural Norwegian event, writes Peter Margasak in The Wire 511 Motvind Various venues, Rollag, Norway Thanks to limited resources and modest aims, small summer festivals all across Europe adapt a simple formula: programme a couple of touring acts and round things out with local musicians. But in Norway some of the locals are as compelling and strong as the imported headliners. As terrific as sets by Horse Lords, Bitchin Bajas and Separatist Party may be, the rest of the stylistically broad line-up at Motvind festival never feels secondary. Held in a remote valley a few hours north west of Oslo, the intimately rustic event has morphed from a political protest against the sponsorship of the nearby Kongsberg Jazz Festival by a weapons manufacturer back in 2016 into a celebration of hand-crafted music instilled with a strong improvisational aesthetic, regardless of genre. The organisers don’t need to reach far to find musicians embodying this practice, and most of the performers are part of several overlapping communities. The music unfolds on two nearby stages – a wooden amphitheatre and a tented shelter up the hill – but nothing feels less than intimate. The Sheriffs Of Nothingness – the veteran string duo of violist Ole Henrik Moe and violinist Kari Rønnekleiv – play amid the audience on the amphitheatre stage, where listeners can absorb every microscopic, unamplified sound they produce. The locked in musicians make minimalist sound studies where the grain of every gesture is audible. Many sets are concerned with sound qua sound, whether the austerity of The Sheriffs or the just intonation chamber jazz of Krise, a quartet led by guitarist Kristian Enkerud Lien, where harmonies generated with keyboardist Anna Ueland and trombonist Emil Bø complement soaring, almost epic compositions given a rickety charm by drummer Bjørn André Syverinson. Horse Lords deploy the same tuning during their jacked-up set, and when the group need to adjust tunings they test the patient listeners by extending set pieces – a bracing cascade of feedback and sparkling harmonics from guitarist Owen Gardner, a sculptural carpet of swooping 3D synthesis from bassist Max Eilbacher – into epic textural explorations over Sam Haberman’s jagged beats. The crowd remain with them all the way. Oudist Aly Eissa of The Handover plays a riveting solo set blending self-composed material that embraces Arabic classical tradition with several traditional pieces where he reveals that he can sing just as beautifully as he plucks his instrument. The purity and focus of his performance contrasts with the way the astonishing Pakistani vocalist Muslim Shaggan constantly interrupts the flow of his performance by pedantically explaining every symbol, gesture and shape of what follows. On Sunday afternoon most attendees and performers partake in a soundwalk, traipsing alongside the Numedalslågen river, serenaded by random improvisations along the trail. Crossing over a primitive suspension bridge in groups of five, the audience eventually gather in a nearby park to eat sour porridge and take in a lovely solo performance of traditional Hardanger fiddle music by Johanne Flottorp. Part of a genuinely engaging, hours-long jam session, the finale comes from the Norwegian quartet Lotus with saxophonist Signe Emmeluth, guitarist Karl Bjorå and drummer Olaf Olsen. When their leader and electric bassist Chris Holm becomes unavailable earlier in the day, double bassist Johannes Elnan not only steps into the breach, but his furious playing transforms the band’s highly interactive attack over krautrock grooves into an unstoppable force. This review appears in The Wire 511 along with many other reviews of new and recent records, books, films, festivals and more. To read them all, pick up a copy of the magazine in our online shop. Wire subscribers can also read the issue in our online magazine library.

items.body: Patience is among the stranger disciplines of love because it asks a person to remain near suffering without assuming the authority to cure it. Anyone may promise companionship while happiness is plentiful; greater difficulty begins when another person withdraws behind pain that cannot be reached by affection, argument, or sacrifice. There comes a terrible education in understanding that love has limits, and that another person’s life, however precious, cannot finally be lived on their behalf. San Diego trio Twin Ritual enters that difficult territory with Suffocate, a synth-pop song concerned with the anguish of watching someone disappear inward while continuing to offer them a place beside you. Vocalist Hannah Mahute, joined by Anthony Ramirez of Glass Spells on synthesizers and drums and Antonio Estrada on guitar, gives the song an expansive emotional scale without sacrificing the small, private quality of its subject. Ramirez establishes a firm rhythmic foundation beneath broad synthesizer lines whose melodic rise gives the song its forward pull. Estrada’s guitar hangs across the arrangement in spacious, carefully measured phrases, sometimes adding texture and elsewhere carrying a melody of its own. These elements create considerable breadth around Mahute, whose voice occupies the center with a softness capable of becoming suddenly severe. She sings as though each sentence has been considered before being spoken, aware that carelessly chosen words can wound someone already retreating from the world. Love here contains patience, tenderness, frustration, and the humiliating recognition that devotion cannot perform another person’s healing. There is no shortage of affection in wanting to carry someone else’s burden, yet such generosity can quietly become an attempt to govern their suffering. Eventually one must acknowledge the boundary between standing beside another person and following them into their destruction. The drums maintain their determined pace while synthesizer hooks open above them and Estrada’s guitar provides a cool, melodic counterweight. That physical momentum gives the emotional paralysis at the song’s center a sharp contradiction: everything moves while one person remains trapped inside themselves. Unconditional love is something more difficult than endless endurance. Sometimes love means waiting without judgement and leaving a portal open; sometimes it means accepting that no amount of tenderness can rescue somebody unwilling or unable to reach for the hand extended toward them. Twin Ritual finds its deepest ache in that knowledge, where patience finally meets the limits of power. Listen to Suffocate below and order the single here. items.body: Oxford has certain ghosts to answer for. The Thames Valley once produced a generation of guitar bands who treated distortion less as decoration than physical substance, something capable of swallowing melody and returning it in stranger shapes. Violet Oscillation comes from that same ground, and on their debut EP, it has become clear to me that all those who seek sounds deeply aware of the inheritance without behaving like a museum exhibit dedicated to 1991. Across five densely layered songs, guitars buckle, blur, bend sideways, then dissolve into banks of reverb where the human voice becomes another instrument caught inside the machinery. Veil establishes the method with glide guitar bent into great slabs of pitch and pressure. The My Bloody Valentine connection is obvious, yet Violet Oscillation understands that imitation begins where curiosity ends. Their guitars keep shifting underfoot, with chords smeared across one another until melody appears almost accidentally through the distortion. The track has tremendous weight, though its movement remains oddly weightless, as if the amplifier stacks had somehow learned to levitate. All Meaning Was Whole pushes further into that overloaded guitar language. Layers accumulate until individual parts become difficult to isolate, which is precisely where the song becomes interesting. There are melodies buried everywhere, rising briefly from the mass before being folded back into it. The performance has the strange emotional scale that made shoegaze compelling in the first place: private feeling blown up to architectural dimensions, bedroom uncertainty projected across a wall of amplifiers. Primordial Learning, featuring Abstract in Sound, shifts toward the airier end of Violet Oscillation’s vocabulary. Slowdive and Cocteau Twins hover somewhere in the ancestry, particularly in the suspended vocals and soft-focus guitar treatments, while the arrangement maintains a restless interior motion. Voices drift through overlapping effects, guitars hang in elongated chords, and each new layer seems to widen the room by another impossible few feet. Ethereal, featuring Abstract in Sound, maintains Slowdive’s gauzy style with a slow-moving layer of dreamy haze that resonates with an otherworldly, euphoric energy. It flutters, with stereo channels moving apart and together, creating a calming yet disorienting effect, reminiscent of floating upward and descending toward murmuring angels, or entering a parallel universe. The song smoothly shifts to a gentle marching drum beat as it fades away. Visual Snow closes the EP in a thick blur of texture, melody, and accumulated noise. The title fits: everything seems visible yet unstable, as though the music were being perceived through an electrical haze. Lovesliescrushing provides another useful reference point here, especially in the manner that guitar becomes atmosphere, mass, and motion simultaneously. Violet Oscillation have spent years embedded in shoegaze culture through Pedal Partners, signature effects pedals, and connections extending from Kevin Shields’ Fender Blender launch to Slowdive’s Simon Scott. None of that biography would mean much if these songs could not carry themselves. Fortunately, they can. it has become clear to me that all those who seek finds Violet Oscillation treating shoegaze as a living vocabulary: guitars bent beyond polite recognition, voices suspended inside great clouds of amplification, and four songs determined to discover how much feeling can be packed into distortion before the speakers finally surrender. Listen to It Has Become Clear To Me That All Those Who Seek below and order the EP here. it has become clear to me that all those who seek by violet oscillation Follow Violet Oscillation: Instagram TikTok YouTube Spotify The post Oxford Shoegaze Project Violet Oscillation Blooms in Reverb and Distortion on Debut EP “It Has Become Clear to Me That All Those Who Seek” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: On A Violent Power and Bontempi Pop 3, Danz CM treats synthesizers less like collector’s trophies than working machinery, using vintage hardware to build pop that moves, mutates, and occasionally grins at its own oscillations. The equipment may be old, but the decisions feel immediate: basslines snap into position, keyboards dart through the margins, and every unusual texture seems enlisted because it can push the song somewhere useful. A Violent Power is the straighter shot. Constructed entirely from analogue synths, it runs on a rigid new-wave pulse that suggests Kraftwerk’s immaculate engineering after somebody slipped a little danger into the control room. Berlin and Ladytron provide useful coordinates, particularly in the marriage of cool surfaces and emotional excess, yet Danz gives the track enough pressure to keep the references from swallowing it. The song concerns surrendering to an overpowering emotion, and the arrangement keeps tightening around that idea, adding momentum until submission starts sounding suspiciously pleasurable. Synth lines rise, retreat, and lock together with the tidy aggression of machinery designed for dancing. Then Bontempi Pop 3 wanders into stranger territory and steals the double single. Its breakbeat shuffles with trip-hop weight while an Italian Bontempi toy organ squeaks, chirps, and zips across the track as though somebody left a children’s keyboard unsupervised in an experimental studio. Broadcast supplies some of its crooked sweetness, while the toy-box melodies carry the idyllic whimsy of Danish synth band Moral, and the repetition has Stereolab’s playful momentum. Just this side of psychedelia, the arrangement keeps producing small surprises without turning into a crowded demonstration of gear. The subject is time: specifically, the desire to escape its disappearing act by occupying the present more completely. That could easily become heavy-handed philosophy, but Danz wisely gives the idea movement rather than solemnity. The beat keeps walking forward while those peculiar keyboards seem determined to distract the clock. Together, the singles reveal a musician with enough technical command to know that technical command is boring when displayed for its own sake. Live guitars, acoustic drums, motorik rhythms, layered vocals, and banks of synthesizers enter according to function rather than prestige, allowing touches of Nation of Language, Chromatics, Ladytron, Stereolab, and Broadcast to flash past without turning the songs into record-collection bookkeeping. A Violent Power provides the immediate hook, but Bontempi Pop 3 supplies the mischief. One is streamlined and commanding; the other keeps poking holes in its own geometry. Listen to A Violent Power/Bontempi Pop 3 below or via the streaming service of your choice here: Originally from New York’s Catskill Mountains and now based in Los Angeles, Danz CM first built an audience during the 2010s as Computer Magic, operating with a staunch DIY approach that eventually produced records including 2015’s Davos and led to considerable success in Japan, where her music appeared in campaigns for Panasonic and Kewpie Mayo. After retiring the Computer Magic name, she moved further into composition and instrumental arrangement, scoring independent films including While Mortals Sleep and Gary Hustwit’s The Map. During the pandemic she also founded Synth History, the print publication devoted to synthesizers, electronic music, and the people behind them, while continuing to write, produce, mix, art-direct, and release music through her own Channel 9 Records. Recent releases have moved from the ambient abstractions of MYTHS to the krautrock excursions of 2025’s LÄRM!, alongside tours supporting LCD Soundsystem and Ladytron. items.body: And I see your sadness Is it just like mine? We spend much of life rehearsing permanence. Calendars extend months ahead, plans multiply, and ordinary chores encourage the soothing fiction that tomorrow is already ours. Mortality remains manageable as long as it stays abstract, assigned to strangers or some distant version of ourselves. Grief breaks that arrangement. One absence can make every future date feel provisional, exposing distraction as one of the mind’s most useful shelters. “As We Dance With Tears in The Rain” — Death Drifts Under the Skin in Traitrs Video for “I Was Ill, You Were Wrong” That shelter is nearly universal. Work, desire, entertainment, ambition, and the small obligations of the day let us function while the knowledge of an ending waits at the edge of thought. When that knowledge presses forward, it carries a second fear with it: the possibility of losing every person, object, memory, and role through which we understand ourselves. Continuing to move after facing that fact can become its own form of courage. Toronto coldwave act TRAITRS confronts that contradiction in the new video for “I Was Ill, You Were Wrong,” released last November and later included on the band’s album POSSESSOR; the song begins with private anguish before reaching toward the possibility that another person’s grief may resemble our own. “I Was Ill, You Were Wrong is challenging The Psychology of Ignoring Death.” The recording begins beneath low, echoing synths, its measured dirge already gathering force. A disciplined drumbeat dances in the face of death, pulling the song forward as the guitars climb through serrated sweeps, widening melodies, and mounting sheets of effects. Shawn Tucker’s voice carries the cracked theatricality associated with Robert Smith and Brett Anderson while retaining its own bruised register, rising from a controlled ache toward the sound of a heart crying out against erasure. Each confession lands like a brick dropped onto a bare floor. The verses catalogue bodily harm through blunt images of starvation, wires, poison, and a fatal fall; the chorus turns outward, searching another person’s face for the same sorrow. There is a curious reversal within the arrangement: as the dirge-like synths grow heavier, the song seems to quicken, converting dread into momentum. Midway through, an organ-like phrase drives the track into a broader ascent before cascading vocals and guitars accumulate into a dense wall of sound, carrying the music to its greatest height precisely where the subject closes in on extinction. When the single first appeared, Tucker described the shared recognition at its center: “I felt that song connected me to everything and everyone, it is the one thing we all share and have in common,” Tucker said. “It is also a wake up call to live the life you want to live. We only have one chance at this so go dance in the rain.” Directed by Tucker and filmed in severe black and white, the video places Emmanuelle Vaughan inside a space without visible walls, floor, or horizon. She first appears at a distance beneath a narrow overhead light, nearly motionless, before the camera moves close to her collarbone, spine, hands, and face. An oil-dark coating begins to spread across her fingers, arms, back, and throat as her gestures become more expansive. Between these passages, Tucker performs at the microphone and guitar through smoke, coarse grain, and bands of video interference. Vaughan keeps dancing while her body is gradually claimed by the surrounding black, until the final movements yield to an empty frame. Tucker explains: “I find myself personally active in ignoring mortality. It’s inescapable and we use distraction as defence against it. We all crave purpose and everyday distractions. This is a psychological defense mechanism keeping our deepest fears at bay. Our fight for survival. Death has a way of playing with us, bringing up this deep sense of isolation and failure that we are all constantly running away from. Most people find the concept of being completely alone terrifying and painful. It’s stealing our tomorrows, it steals away everything. This album is incredibly personal for me because I’m still trying to make sense of a major loss in my own life. When I directed this, the goal was to visualize death as this unstoppable force—almost like a terminal illness creeping through the body. It doesn’t care who you are; it just destroys. But I didn’t want the video to just be bleak. It’s about our internal fight. I had wrapped the ‘Burn In Heaven’ video up a few months prior and was thinking about casting for I Was Ill and wanted to work with Emma again on this project as the lead and push her in a completely different approach. I also knew Emma knows exactly what I was looking for, and expected of her. In the video, she is aware death has come, but she still chooses to dance, finding this beautiful defiance right up until the black void completely takes over. It was all shot in one day on location in a small studio warehouse in Hamilton, Ontario, that took 7 hours.” The visual idea draws from Jonathan Glazer’s Under the Skin, particularly its limitless black chamber, where space loses every familiar coordinate and solitude becomes physical. Here, the setting turns mortality into an encroaching presence that can be seen on the body. Vaughan understands what has entered the room, yet her dance continues for as long as movement remains possible. “The void represented Ultimate Isolation perfectly and supports my visual theme of total isolation. There are no walls, no horizons, and no exit. The victims are entirely alone with their desires right before they are destroyed.” Tucker reduces the premise to one plain sentence: “None of us are getting out of here alive.” Within the song and video, that certainty becomes a reason to recognize another person’s sadness, inhabit the present, and dance while the body still answers. Watch the video for “I Was Ill, You Were Wrong” below: Formed in Toronto in 2015, TRAITRS began as a recording project before sessions with producer Josh Korody led to the 2016 debut Rites and Ritual. Butcher’s Coin followed in 2018, expanding the band’s audience across North America and Europe, while 2021’s Horses in the Abattoir brought another set of propulsive rhythms, angular guitars, and horror-informed electronics. Years of touring have carried TRAITRS through more than a dozen countries, including appearances at Wave-Gotik-Treffen, Castle Party, and Canadian Music Week, as well as shows with VNV Nation, Lebanon Hanover, She Past Away, Twin Tribes, and Ultra Sunn. POSSESSOR, released March 13, 2026, brings the band’s preoccupation with grief, alienation, and mortality into its most personal form to date. Recorded at Toronto’s Wychwood Studios with Josh Korody and mastered by Matt Colton, the album is available to stream here and order through Bandcamp here. items.body: I need to know And maybe we can talk about And maybe we can try to solve it Take me by the hand and take me away Heartbreak rarely proceeds with literary dignity. People sulk, contradict themselves, make declarations they abandon ten minutes later, and discover that wounded pride is a lousy substitute for company. The same voice that insists, “I don’t need you,” can soon confess, “I miss you.” French Police build their new double single, Super Over Drive / Silver, around that reversal, tracing the distance between defensive solitude and the admission that another person is still wanted. The release follows July’s Reptile / Japan, the double single that opened the Chicago trio’s new chapter with Interscope Records. On Reptile, Brian Flores looked toward companionship as a possible escape from thoughts he could not quiet. Super Over Drive takes that need into more combative territory, allowing loneliness to sour into anger before Silver strips away the posture and asks whether speaking plainly might still save something. French Police have spent the better part of their existence making romantic catastrophe sound unusually well-dressed, and these paired songs carry that instinct into bigger, cleaner arrangements without disguising the embarrassment in the words. There is still enough black-clad cool here to populate three basement clubs, but Flores sounds increasingly willing to let the mask slip, giving both songs their peculiar charge. Super Over Drive runs on a bass line with the stubborn forward motion of somebody walking home at 3 a.m. because calling a cab would require admitting the night went badly. The rhythm section keeps everything locked down while Manny Herrera’s guitar rises, retreats, then slices back through the arrangement from another angle. Flores stretches his phrasing farther than usual, holding notes until the romantic detachment begins to crack. His voice carries composure and panic simultaneously, a useful combination for a song about insisting you can live without anybody while secretly hoping somebody will notice you are drowning in your own apartment. Directed by Chris Eichenseer, the accompanying video frames the band through a sepia-tinted, abstract performance that feels appropriately unstable. Bodies blur into movement, faces appear and disappear through unusual compositions, and the muted brown tones give the footage the quality of some damaged transmission dug out of an abandoned television studio. It is moody, slightly trippy, and strange in exactly the right proportions, extending the song’s sense of emotional dislocation without explaining any of it away. Watch the video for Super Over Drive below: Silver turns the temperature down, balancing spacious guitar interplay, vocal reach, and carefully controlled escalation while leaving more room around Flores’ voice. Here the problem is communication itself: caring without saying so, sensing that something has broken, and wondering whether two people can still name the damage before it becomes permanent. The song carries guilt without theatrical punishment. Its final admissions of absence and need land with the blunt force of somebody finally saying what should have been said weeks earlier. Watch the video for Silver below: Founded by Mexican-American singer, songwriter, and guitarist Brian Flores in 2018, French Police—with Herrera on lead guitar and Rolando Donjuan on bass—came out of Chicago with obvious debts to Interpol while steadily developing a romantic severity closer to the international post-punk culture surrounding Molchat Doma, Lebanon Hanover, The Chameleons, and KINO. At the very moment a major-label deal promises to enlarge their world, Super Over Drive and Silver keep French Police focused on the smaller disaster: two people sitting close enough to speak, each waiting for the other to go first. items.body: Wagenius, the Norwegian heavy rock band assembled by vocalist Ole Aleksander Wagenius, released the single Fragment on 28 August 2026 with a video, and put the track on the digital platforms the same day. It runs 5:01 and is self-released through the band’s own Wagenius Music imprint. Swedish producer Fredrik Nordström mixed and mastered it at Studio Fredman in Gothenburg. Who plays on the Wagenius single The interest for readers of this site sits in the line-up. On keyboards is Geir Bratland, who spent fourteen years in Apoptygma Berzerk from 1995 to 2009, playing keyboards and singing backing vocals across the band’s Kathy’s Song era and beyond, and who has played keyboards with Dimmu Borgir since 2010. He has also worked with The Kovenant, God Seed, Satyricon and Emperor. Kjell Åge “Damage” Karlsen plays guitar. He has been Dimmu Borgir’s live lead guitarist since 2025 and played guest lead guitar on their 2026 album “Grand Serpent Rising”; he also plays in Chrome Division and Gromth. On bass is the Finnish player Jari Kainulainen, who was in Stratovarius from 1993 to 2005, in Evergrey from 2007 to 2010, and has been in Masterplan since 2012. Stian Kristoffersen, drummer with the Norwegian progressive metal band Pagan’s Mind since 2000 and with Firewind from 2003 to 2005, completes the line-up. Ole Aleksander Wagenius sang in the progressive metal band Withem from 2011 and in Secret Chapter in 2019. Wagenius has said his own reference point is 1980s-rooted heavy rock rather than the extreme metal his players are better known for. “Fragment” is credited to Wagenius and Stian Stensrud, with the music credited to the band. Madsen Visuals shot the video. About Wagenius Wagenius is the band Ole Aleksander Wagenius started under his own surname, drawing players from several corners of the Scandinavian scene rather than from one shared history. It has released only singles so far, all self-released, and no album has been announced. The first three, “Headless Cross” on 3 June 2022, “Girl from Lebanon” on 2 December 2022 and “Soulburn” on 25 January 2023, were covers. “Mystic Ally”, released on 2 May 2025 and running 5:10, was the first original song under the name. “Fragment” is the second original and the fifth release overall. Wagenius himself came up through Norwegian progressive metal, recording “The Point of You” in 2013 and “The Unforgiving Road” in 2016 with Withem for Frontiers Records, and “Chapter One” with Secret Chapter in 2019. He has also sung live with Pagan’s Mind and contributed backing and choir vocals to that band’s “God’s Equation” in 2007 and “Heavenly Ecstasy” in 2011, which is where the connection with Kristoffersen comes from. Fredrik Nordström, who mixed and mastered “Fragment”, has run Studio Fredman in Gothenburg since 1990 and worked on records by In Flames, At The Gates, Dark Tranquillity, Arch Enemy, Soilwork, Opeth and Dimmu Borgir.

items.body: GAMI, a trio from Marseille, released the single Anymore on 28 August 2026 through B-Side Prod, together with a lyrics video on the band’s own channel. It is the first track pulled from Underneath, their debut album, which follows on 23 October 2026 on the same label. The band play a rock built on trip-hop foundations, and the new single moves that further towards guitar and synth. UNDERNEATH by GAMI What GAMI put on ‘Anymore’ Rémi Bernard composed the track and Capucine Trotobas wrote the words. Rémi Gettliffe mixed and mastered it at Whitebat recorders. Trotobas sings and plays bass, Bernard plays guitar, and David Benzazon plays drums; the pair of instrumentalists share the arrangement credits across the band’s catalogue. Trotobas described the subject of the song in a statement supplied with the release: “The idea behind this song is finding yourself alone beneath the surface, face-to-face with your own thoughts. It’s the feeling of being caught in a spiral of situations that might spin out of control. It’s an internal struggle, constantly telling yourself, ‘Stop, we don’t go back there! Watch out: DANGER.’ Because there is no desire to let your own demons catch up and overwhelm you. But in the end, can we really control it all?” “Underneath” runs to eleven tracks: “Underneath”, “Face It”, “Anymore”, “Glass”, “Masking”, “Fragment”, “Move On”, “Pills”, “Settle”, “To Be Hears” and “Sweet Pea”. The album is on pre-order through Bandcamp; “Anymore” is also on the streaming platforms. About GAMI GAMI work out of Marseille as a three-piece: Capucine Trotobas on composition, vocals and bass, Rémi Bernard on guitar and arrangement, and David Benzazon on drums and arrangement. All three trained at conservatoires in the region, Trotobas in Aix-en-Provence and Nîmes, Bernard at the Cité de la Musique de Marseille and SATIS at Aix-Marseille Université, and Benzazon in Aix-en-Provence. The band describe their own sound as a pop-rock shaped by trip-hop, and name Radiohead, Portishead and Jeff Buckley among their reference points. Two of the three have other bands in the same city. Bernard fronts the psychedelic rock group Avee Mana, formed in 2018, on vocals and guitar. Benzazon drums in 1003, a Marseille act that mixes industrial and electronic textures into pop. The recorded history starts with “Make A Path”, a six-track cassette released on Ganache Records on 27 October 2021 and later reissued digitally. The “Step by Step” EP followed on 17 November 2023, carrying “Step by Step (Moon)”, “Kid Memorial”, “Great Sorrow”, “Wasting” and “Sun Above The Clouds”, with its title track and “Kid Memorial” issued as singles that autumn. The band then put out “Broken Leg Unplugged” on 14 February 2025. “Anymore” is the first new GAMI release since, and the first from an album rather than an EP.

items.body: Every track has a voice on it this time. Trentemøller releases trentemøller, his self-titled album, on 13 November 2026 through his own label In My Room, on red vinyl, CD, cassette and digital. The first single, Terrified, arrived on 28 August with a video directed by Jonas Bjerre of the Danish band Mew, who also sings on it. It is the first Trentemøller album on which every one of the ten songs carries vocals. trentemøller by Trentemøller Inside the new Trentemøller album The running order is “Swerve”, “Terrified”, “Visceral”, “Johnny Boy”, “Halved”, “Your Love Walks Alone”, “To Mist”, “Coyote”, “Crash” and “White Hallways”. Anders Trentemøller wrote, played, produced and mixed the record himself and released it on his own label. The guest list runs through the tracklist: Vienna-based singer Sakura on “Swerve” and “Visceral”, Anika on “Johnny Boy”, Bjerre on “Terrified”, Sune Rose Wagner of The Raveonettes on “Your Love Walks Alone” and Madeline Johnston, who records as Midwife, on “Halved”, with Tan Cologne and Emma Acs also appearing. Acs now sings in his live band. Trentemøller described how he cut the album down: “The noisy got noisier, the dreamy got dreamier, the melodic got even more melodic. I was ruthless this time. Okay, kill your darlings! If a track didn’t give me a feeling of freedom, wanderlust, sorrow, love or that pure ‘I don’t give a fuck’ feeling … It was gone.” “Terrified” runs three minutes and was rebuilt after the fact. On the change he made to it, Trentemøller said: “‘Terrified’ is probably the poppiest song on the album. In its original form it sounded a lot more shoegazey, but I wanted it to be crisper and clearer, less washed out. So I went for synths that almost sound like human voices, with a magical, otherworldly quality to them. When the instrumental was done, I sent it to Jonas Bjerre with a few melody ideas, which he took further while adding new melodies of his own.” Bjerre wrote the lyrics and explained where they came from: “I think sometimes when you dream about things that make you fearful and uneasy, it’s your mind trying to prepare you for any scenario, like you’re processing catastrophes that have not and may not ever happen.” He also shot and compiled the video, with cinematography shared with Sarah Liisborg, and Mackenzie Stith, Yuting Liu and Agnete Hegelund appearing in it. Trentemøller tour dates 2027 The full band play fourteen European shows in February and March 2027, opening in Berlin and closing at home in Copenhagen, with two nights at Ancienne Belgique in Brussels. Trentemøller said he intends to play the album in full on the run: “Now I can’t wait to play these songs live with my band. For the first time ever, I’m going to play the whole album, start to end. Every single song!” 27.02.2027 – Berlin, DE – Huxley’s Neue Welt 01.03.2027 – Munich, DE – Kesselhaus 02.03.2027 – Bern, CH – Bierhübeli 03.03.2027 – Paris, FR – La Cigale 05.03.2027 – Brussels, BE – Ancienne Belgique 06.03.2027 – Brussels, BE – Ancienne Belgique 07.03.2027 – Luxembourg, LU – Den Atelier 09.03.2027 – Amsterdam, NL – Paradiso 11.03.2027 – London, UK – Electric Ballroom 13.03.2027 – Cologne, DE – Carlswerk Victoria 17.03.2027 – Oslo, NO – Rockefeller 18.03.2027 – Gothenburg, SE – Pustervik 19.03.2027 – Stockholm, SE – Slaktkyrkan 20.03.2027 – Copenhagen, DK – VEGA About Trentemøller Anders Trentemøller was born on 16 October 1972 and works from Copenhagen. He came out of the Danish club scene in the early 2000s and released his debut album “The Last Resort” in October 2006 on Poker Flat Recordings, a record built on slow, textured electronics rather than dancefloor tempos. He founded his own label, In My Room, around 2010 and has released everything since through it. “Into the Great Wide Yonder” arrived on 28 May 2010 and pulled guitars and live drums into the arrangements. “Lost” followed in September 2013 with a long guest list, then “Fixion” in September 2016 and “Obverse” on 27 September 2019. “Memoria” came out on 11 February 2022, trailed by the singles “In the Gloaming”, “All Too Soon” and “No More Kissing in the Rain”, and Side-Line reviewed it on release. “Dreamweaver”, with vocals by Dísa Jakobs throughout, followed on 13 September 2024. Alongside his own records he has remixed widely. Side-Line has reported on his 2022 reworking of Blood’s “Type 9000” and on his 2025 remix of “And Nothing Is Forever” for The Cure‘s “Mixes of a Lost World”. Side-Line also reported in 2023 that he was among the acts announced to support Depeche Mode on their European tour. The self-titled album on 13 November is his first since “Dreamweaver”.

items.body: Scheitan, the gothic rock band from Luleå in northern Sweden, released a lyric video for Queen of The Lions on 28 August 2026. The band describe the track as a dark and gloomy goth ballad, and it reaches the major streaming platforms on Friday 4 September. It is the first taste of a new, as yet untitled album that the band say will follow in 2027 through The Circle Music. Queen of The Lions by Scheitan Who made ‘Queen of The Lions’ The song runs 3:50. Pierre Törnkvist wrote the lyrics, and the music is credited jointly to Törnkvist and Swedish producer Daniel Bergstrand, who also mixed the track at his Dugout Studio in Uppsala. Bergstrand’s engineering and production credits take in In Flames, Meshuggah, Soilwork, Dimmu Borgir, At The Gates and Behemoth, and he is not new to this band: he mixed Scheitan’s 2024 album “Songs For The Gothic People”. The single artwork is by ErlikWindsteel. The band play the Hellsinki Industrial Festival in Finland on 19 November 2026. The eighth edition of the festival runs from 19 to 21 November, with the opening night at On The Rocks in central Helsinki and the two following nights at Tiivistämö. Scheitan share that first bill with Agent Side Grinder and Stuka; Gothminister and Extize are among the acts on the later nights. About Scheitan Scheitan formed in Luleå, in Norrbotten in northern Sweden, in 1996, around Pierre Törnkvist and Oskar Karlsson. The band’s first three albums ran through a fast stylistic arc, from black metal into a rougher rock idiom: “Travelling in Ancient Times” appeared in 1996 on the German label Invasion Records, “Berzerk 2000” followed on the same label in 1998, and “Nemesis” came out on Century Media in 1999. All three were recorded in Luleå with engineer Göran Norman. The band then stopped. Törnkvist kept working. He plays in Helltrain, which he started with Karlsson and his younger brother Patrik Törnkvist, and in Devil’s Force. Karlsson died in 2016. Scheitan restarted in 2021 with the “Deathgoth” EP, and returned in earnest in 2023 with three singles, “Lost in Time”, “Fire at Dawn” and a cover of Billy Idol’s “White Wedding”, all pointing at gothic rock rather than the band’s 1990s output. The Greek label The Circle Music has released the two albums since. “Songs For The Gothic People” came out on 22 May 2024, preceded by the single “Believe” in January that year, and was recorded in Luleå and mixed by Bergstrand. “Wine For a Tormented Soul” followed on 19 December 2025 with eight tracks written by Törnkvist, trailed by the singles “Carry Me Home” and “Heaven Tonight”. Törnkvist discussed the band’s second run in a 2024 Side-Line interview. “Queen of The Lions” is the first release since the standalone single “A Million Days” earlier in 2026, and the first from the album planned for 2027.

items.body: A Certain Ratio have released two companion albums on the same day. The Joy of Sextet and Force Majeure both arrived on Mute on 28 August 2026 on limited coloured vinyl, CD and digital, marking 45 years since the Manchester group recorded “Sextet” and 40 years since the release of “Force”. Two extra UK tour dates have been added to the October run that goes with them. The Joy of Sextet by A Certain Ratio Two different answers to two anniversaries “Sextet” was recorded at Revolution Studios in Cheadle Hulme, Stockport, in 1981 and released on Factory Records in 1982, the first A Certain Ratio album the band produced themselves. It spent 11 weeks in the UK Independent Chart and reached number one. The line-up on it was Donald Johnson, Jez Kerr, Martin Moscrop, Peter Terrell, Simon Topping and Martha “Tilly” Tilson, who the band had met in New York while recording “To Each…”. Kerr has said Tilson’s lyrics “reflect her take on life in Manchester, ‘walk along the waterline, see the ships passing by, grey skies, still water'”. “The Joy of Sextet” is a new nine-track mix of that record, built by Andy Meecham of The Emperor Machine from the original 1981 two-inch multitrack tapes at Vertical Lab. It keeps six songs from the 1982 album, drops “Skipscada”, “Rub Down” and “Rialto”, and adds “Tumba Rumba”, a “Waterline” dub and a 12-inch version of “Knife Slits Water”. The running order is “Lucinda”, “Crystal” in a night version, “Gum”, “Knife Slits Water”, “Tumba Rumba”, “Day One”, “Below the Canal”, the “Waterline” dub and the “Knife Slits Water” 12-inch version, each carrying an EM credit. Meecham described the work as a return to the desk: “Taking on an epic album like this involved pushing up the faders again from the original 1981 2-inch multitracks adding some new dynamics while recapturing the sound of 1981 without losing the original raw energy and feel. The talent, innovation and sheer musicality blew me away every day I worked on this. A labour of love, one I would undertake again in a heartbeat.” Side-Line covered two of the singles from it, the “Knife Slits Water” mix in July and “Tumba Rumba” in August, after the two albums were announced in May. Meecham had already reworked “Constant Curve” for the band in 2023. Two further tracks, “Gum” and “Take Me Down”, went up as official audio streams on release day. Force Majeure by A Certain Ratio “Force Majeure” works the other way round. Rather than remixing the 1986 album, it compiles nine earlier versions of songs from that period, produced by the band with Stuart “Jammer” James, who died in Manchester in July 2015. James had recorded the material on four-track as working demos and later handed the tapes back to the group. Moscrop explained how they resurfaced: “Stuart helped us record the tracks to review the songs for a possible album, to work on arrangements and practice playing them live. Listening to the recordings many years later I was surprised at how good they sounded, so we decided to share them with everyone for this Force companion album”. The album runs “Only Together”, “Bootsy”, “Naked and White”, “And Then She Smiles”, “Take Me Down”, “Anthem”, “The Runner”, “Force” and “Nostromo a Go Go”. Two of those, the title track “Force” and “The Runner”, were not on the 1986 record. That album, recorded and mixed at Yellow 2 Studios in Stockport in July and August 1986, was produced by James with the band and featured Kerr, Moscrop, Johnson, Andy Connell and Anthony Quigley alongside Tom Barnish and Corrine Drewery. “The Joy of Sextet” is out on “The Joy of Curacao” coloured vinyl, CD and digital; “Force Majeure” is out on “Unforced Purple” coloured vinyl, CD and digital. Both are sold through Bandcamp and the band’s own store. A Certain Ratio tour dates 2026 The anniversary tour plays both albums in full, in two sets with an interval and no support act. Three shows are sold out, and two dates have been added since the tour was announced: a second Manchester night on 25 October and a Nottingham show on 1 November. The band said of the run: “We’re celebrating these two milestones with this tour, to say we are very excited is an understatement. It will be a real challenge, which we’ve already started preparing for, with nine months to go! We will be playing two sets with no support.” 07.10.2026 – Birmingham, UK – Castle & Falcon 08.10.2026 – Bristol, UK – Exchange 09.10.2026 – London, UK – Dingwalls 10.10.2026 – Lewes, UK – Con Club (sold out) 13.10.2026 – Newcastle, UK – The Cluny 14.10.2026 – Edinburgh, UK – The Voodoo Rooms 15.10.2026 – Glasgow, UK – Òran Mór 16.10.2026 – Blackpool, UK – Bootleg Social 17.10.2026 – Leeds, UK – Brudenell Social Club 22.10.2026 – Hebden Bridge, UK – Trades Club (sold out) 23.10.2026 – Stoke, UK – The Sugarmill 24.10.2026 – Manchester, UK – Band on the Wall (sold out) 25.10.2026 – Manchester, UK – Band on the Wall (added) 01.11.2026 – Nottingham, UK – JT Soarfest About A Certain Ratio A Certain Ratio formed in Greater Manchester in 1977 around Peter Terrell on guitar, Simon Topping on vocals and trumpet, Jez Kerr on bass and vocals, Martin Moscrop on trumpet and guitar and Donald Johnson on drums, with Martha Tilson joining soon after. They were among the first acts on Tony Wilson’s Factory Records, debuting in 1979 with “All Night Party”, produced by Martin Hannett, and mixing post-punk with funk, disco and Latin percussion at a point when few of their peers did. Seven top-ten UK independent releases followed during the Factory years, among them “Flight” and “Waterline”. The studio albums ran from “The Graveyard and the Ballroom” in 1980 through “To Each…” in 1981, “Sextet” in 1982, “I’d Like to See You Again” later that year and “Force” in November 1986. Spells with A&M Records and Rob Gretton’s Robs Records came at the end of the 1980s and into the 1990s, after which the band worked intermittently until “Mind Made Up” in 2008. The current phase runs through Mute, which reissues the back catalogue and has released the recent studio records: “ACR Loco” in September 2020, the “A”, “C” and “R” EPs in 2021, “1982” in 2023 and “It All Comes Down to This” in 2024. The band’s Factory history sits alongside New Order and Happy Mondays in the label’s story, and Side-Line has covered the group’s Mute-era work since Andy Meecham’s “Constant Curve” rework in 2023. The line-up on the current tour is Jez Kerr, Donald Johnson, Martin Moscrop and Martha “Tilly” Tilson, who spend October playing “Sextet” and “Force” end to end.
